div.head: TIT-BITS,
div.p: TIT-BITS,
VICENTRIO MODES OF BURIAL.

The story is told of a certain Ftenchraten who had been a great collector of coins. By tees will he 'directed that his obsequies should be performed -with every accompaniment calculated to inspire marrisful feelings. His body was to be 'wrapped in 'tanned pig-skin and burned coffinloss an a standing !position upon a pile of charcoal. Laurel branches wore to be carried by the mourners, and on return- eing from the church they were to throw open the "chambers in which his treasures were deposited. and all corners were :welcome to balp themselves 'ES they pleased to the coetents. It was a sore disap- pointment to the public, however, to find that before they were admitted, the servants cie the deceased had decamped with everything that was portable. The wishes of a curious character, Who was named Hilkington, better known as Sqaire Hawley, were folly carried out a few years ago at a place near Doncaster. He was burled in his owed garden. amid the graves of his dead cattle, whick had been stricken down by rinderpest. He was laid out in full hunting costume, including spurs and whip, and was planed in a stone coffin weighing upwards of a ton, which had to be lowered into the grave by means of a crane. His old pony was shot and buried at his feet, and at his head were laid the bodies of his favourite dog and an old fox. AU his property was left to lis groom, on condition that these faneral observan-es were fully carried out; in default, the estate was to go to the priest of Don- caster. The groom, however, did ra-A suffer the bequest to himself to lap,e. It is related that a ce.taln crotchety old York- ahireman some years since left directions that on the day of his burial a great public breakfast should be given in the town where he might die, and that his coffin, siting upon towels knotted together, should be borne alcog by relays of men, and "bumped" three times npon a partioalar heap of stones, and that the Lamentation of al:linnet' should then be sung. A still more important provision was made regarding the presence of mourners in the church- yard. Every man, woman, and child, who -entered the ground +with, or alter the procession, had to receive a dole of sixpence. 'Never before or since, we are told, was that churchyard so full of people. A Sasses gentleman, named Jack Fuller, ordered his executors to bury him inn pyramidal mausoleum . in Brightling churchyard. His reason for desiring to be enclosed in stone above ground was his unwillingness to be eaten by his relatives a process he • considered inevitable if buried in the ordinary way. The worms,' be declared, 'would eat me, the ducks would eat the worms, and my relations would eat the claws.' A gentleman, named • Underwood, left £6,000 to his sister on condition that she had him buried in a particular-fashion. Six gentlemen were appointed to follow him to the grave, where they were to sing the last stanza of the twentieth ode of the second Book of Horace. Mourning was forbidden to be worn; to bell had to be tolled, and no relation was to follow 'the corpse. The six chosen gentlemen were to -to the only mourners. The coffin was painted green, and the deceased was buried with his clothes on. Three copies of Horace were placed in the grave with him, together with Bentley's " Milton " and a Greek Testament. After supper, the six mourners sang the ode—all being in strict accordance with the -win 01 the deceased.—Camel/'s Saturday .journal.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NELLIV, Children's dresses this summer are really charm. ing, and, what is of far more importance to the horne.dressMaker, they are, in the majority of oases, simple in cut and trimming. For every-day wear nothingseems more fashionable than frocks of coloured 'Risen or cambric, made with a moderately 'fall straight skirt and eque.re-cut bodice, shoring cuemisette and full sleeves of white lama or fine cambric, withered, tucked, or smockeE according to taste. A pale blue cambric rotted with white, for instance, would make up prettily in this way, the skirt being ornamented with three 'tucks, placed a little distance from the hem, and the top df the dress, Ars well as the 15:etelles which pass over the shoulders, edged with narrow frills. The chemisette and sleeves, which form a com- plete-under-bodice, are smocked with pale blue at threst and wrists. 'Vern with a wide-brimmed rush. hat, simply trimmed with a twist and two big loess rosettes of palerrt blue gauss, such a costume OA this is smart enough for any occasion, especially Ho finishing touch is put to the effect of the whole bz tan stockings and shoes. A pretty style of • washing-dress for o. girl from six to twelve years old—the chemisette frock juat described is more •-suitable for a child under eight —is of brown- .tholland, which is so popular for both children's and 'ladies' dresses tlf.s season. The skirt is kilted and sewn to a rather wide holland Land, and the bodice is coat-shaped, reaching just below the hips, and opening in front to show a loose coloured cotton blouse, which hangs over the waistband like an old-fashioned Garibaldi

Another very pretty dress, but of a rather more elaborate description than the one mentioned above is called the "Dogma" costume, and lie loose dress of nun's viling falling from a yoke of , coloured silk covered with lace. Puffs of silk are • on the sleeves, while lace epaulettes fall over these. This dress is exceedingly pretty in appearance. The "coif bonnet" is one of the season's novelties, and is a suitable shape to go with the large "tea-cake" roll of hair. Then there Is a very flat shape, and one with rolled edges, and, last but not least, a distinctive novelty in the shape of the new era* ribbons that are the latest introduction in the way of millinery. They are of satin-like smoothness, about two inches or more in width. They are plaited as the "basket-braids" of hair used to be, and tied into bows, the ends of which are cut off into pointed ends, exactly as ribbon is treated. A novelty in the way of arti- ficial flowers, or rather fruits, perhaps, is the Indian corn-cob, not of the natural size, but quite big enough. Velvet is more used than anything else as a trimming for both hats and bonnets, and, strange to say, it is no longer hemmed at the edges,_but used raw-edged, just as milliners have been using cloth for some time.

Of all the oonfectlone in•millinery, the one which ,attracted my attention most was a quaint little bonnet of golden-hued straw with the crown set into two peak; and in front of this stand erect a let osprey, with a bow of cream lace, Caught with jewelled pins. The newest shaped sailor hats have rather wide and indented crowns, are made in finely-striped or decked straws in various combinations of colour. They are finished off with bands of ribbon match- ing the darkest colour in the straw, and bows of ribbon on the left side. Wings are again much used in millinery. A new Paris model hat is turned up over the brow like a coronet, and lined with coloured ,velvet. White lace is largely used In millinery, and for summer bonnets has a lighter and more graceful effect than ribbon. It is kept in place (the fans, quillings, and bows) by fine wire. An open lace, rather like horse-hair, is extremely ,pretty, and, cleverly used, looks remarkably airy ,and dressy.

A most faaeinating promenade gown watt of handsome black silk grenadine, made up \ over duchespe satin. Tlic skirt conaisted of three deep flounces, each edged with b4b6 rib on and peeping out from each fold a bunch pf ribboa in the exact imitation of arysanthemums. The corsage, draped cross fashion, had full puffs on sleeves of grenadine, bows on 'boulders of I el é ribbon, also a large buach at waiat-belt.; with collar and bell; of satin.
Yuurs biacerely, JENNIE.

Set Strawberry Cream. Pune a gill of eredm into a basin, and beat It till re- sembling snovr. Then thoroug'dly dissolve an ounce of isinglass in A gill of boiling water. Add this Co the cream. Rub bait & pound of ripe straw brri Les picked from Um

stalk through a celiac, mix altogether and sweeten to taste with castor sugar. Should the cream not be of a perfect colour drop in half a teaspoonful of carmine. Pour the whole in a well-soaked mould and place it on ice or in a cold place for 12 hours. When set serve on a glass dish, Garnish with strawberries laid on their leaves.

Bottling Fruit. quite a simple way of bottling cherries, gooseberries, is simply to gather the fruit when quite dry, put them into bottles which must be filled up with water, tie a piece of bladder over the tops, and place the bottles in a pan with enough cold water in it to come nearly up to the top of the bottles, and place a little hay between them to preventthe bottles breaking. Bring the water gently to boiling point, and then let it continue to boil for seme little time according to the fruit used. Far in- stance, when gooseberries are being bottled the water should boil mntil the fruit just begins at the stem end to crack, and the same thing with regard to cherries or plums. The bottles should be left in the water until they are ecite cold, and must be kept in a cool place. Strawberries and raspberries are better when a syrup is poured into the bottles instead of water. The fruit should be quite 'fresh and as little bruised as possible that is go- ing to be bottled, and the bottles should be quite dry. The syrup must be made by boiling together for a quar- ter of an hour half a pint of water and a pound of loaf sugar, and leave it until cold,when it must be poured en to the fruit in the bottles, which, like those in the recipe given above, must be covered with bladder and placed in a pen with sufficient cold water in it to reach the necks of the bottles; after the waterboils it need only simmer for a few minutes,then be removed from the bre and left until the bottles are cold. French beans can be fairly successfully Itcpt ley placing them freshly gathered,and after removing the ends and'the hard strings from the edges, in earthenware jars, and sprinkle between each layer a little salt. The beans will shrink a good deal after they are put into the jar' and more must be added -so that the jars are quite full before they are covered with bladder. They should be kept in a dry cool place, and before being used must be well soaked in cold water otherwise they will be rather salt, and a good bunch of green parsley should be put in the water they are boiled an. Peas can be hottled very well by mixing a good tea- spoonful of salt with every half gill of water used. Fill the bottles with freshly shelled and gathered peas, and pour the half gill of brine into every pint bottle of peas, cover the bottles and treat in the same way as the fruit only let the peas cook for half an hour. The most im- portant thing is to gather all fruit and vegetables which are to be preserved in very dry, bright weather, and use , quite dry bottles.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 24, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 24, 1893.
Delicate Children.

A wise old physician once said, frankly :" Much more , depends upon the nurse than the physician. We see , the patient but once a day, and a poor nurse can easily undo all the good our medicine does." It is upon the continual care and watchfulness that a good nurse exer- cises, that the mother mustdepend in rearing a delicati child, rather than upon doctors' drugs and lotions. Systematic outdoor •exercise, but never to the point of fatigue, will do mere towards building up the strength than all the tonics. This does not mean that the tonic is not also valuable, but the individual who depends on tonics alone, without proper hygienic care in the sur- rounding of the invalid, is likely to be disappointed in the result. The inability to sleep on the part of some nervous sufferers is often due to close air. When the sick one is too ill to go out in the open air, but can be moved, it is best to have two rooms, one for use at night and one during the day. .Both should be plentifully sup- plied with fresh-air, and the room in use during the day should be bright and sunny., with an open fire burning on the hearth in cold weather, and blooming flowers in the windows. It is not enough for an invalid that his table be supplied with wholesome suitable food, and his room kept warm. The food must look tempting. The room must look cheerful. There must be an atmosphere of rest about the room that will be soothing to the nerves. Tho light must be graduated so that it is neither glaring nor gloomy. The ornaments about the room must be occasionally changed, so that the restless invalid may have something new to take up his attention and divert his thoughts from himself. Still it is foolish to make too many changes or disturb the restful quiet of the room. A nurse should be a person of strong nerve, but one sensitive and intelligent enough to appro. ci Ito and soothe the abnormally sensitive nerves oh the convalescent. It is upon ucli care that the success of nurses' work depends, as well as upon perfect system in the routine performance of their duties.—" New York Tribune."

div.head: PePULA R EVENT.
div.p: A PePULA R EVENT.

On the 17th of April (1860) a contest took place which resounded throughout England. An American boxer named Heenan crossed the seas to show that the new world could produce a pugilist of greater skill and prow- ess than Tom Sayers, who wore the champion belt of England. Heenan was a giant, while his competitor was•corapamtively a man of small stature, but agile. skilful, and watchful. Almost at the commencensent of the fight the English champion had one of his arms dis- abled by a blow he received ; nevertheless he made such good use Of the other arm that Heenan's face was bat- tered into a mass in which it was difficult to discover any trace of the human eoantenance, and he was for the time completely blinded ; and his antogonist was hardly less severely punished. The appearance of the police brought the fight to a premature close. Both claimed the victory, but Sayers kept the champion's belt; and an attempt made to satisfy both of the com- batants by presenting a belt to each was only very parti- ally successful. But our principal reason for recording these circumstances is the immense interest that this fight excited. Half London endeavoured to be witnesses of it; and though comparatively few of thoto who attempted to make their way to the scene' of action succeeded in arriving at it, the number of anctaters was •enormous. But that which will most astonish our posterity to learn is, that peers, members of parliament, clergymen, men o highly-cultivated minds, men remarkable forartistic taste and artistic power, were in the front ranks cif those who witnessed this disgusting, disgraceful, and unla ful exhibition. Savers !nada his public entry into the metropolis through a oast crowd, and amidst most ttunultuous applauses. " Bell's Life in London." boasted that the enthusiasm displayed was greater than would have attended the proclamation of a new king and Lord Palmerston, in his place in the House of Commons, declared that lie saw nothing more demoralising in a boxing match than in the ascent of a balloon ; apparently forgetting that the latter was per- mitted by the law, while the tormer was carried on in direct violation of its well-known provisions. Sayers also made a triumphal entry into Liverposl, where his reception was no less enthusiastic.

div.head: SWANSEA. ELECTION.
div.p: THE SWANSEA. ELECTION.
THE LTBERAL MEMBER: A REMARKABLE CAREER.

Mr. William Williams, the Liberal candidate, was on Monday returned unopposed for Swansea district. It was uncertain up to as lite as one &cock on Monday afternoon whether or not there would be a three-cornered fight. The nomination papers of the three candidates were ready, but the Labour leaders gave way at the last moment, alleging as their reason that if three candidates were in the running the seat would be jeopardised in favour of the Conservative. Sir John Jenkins thereupon withdrew as well, on the ground that to contest the .seat while the Liberals were united would be a hopeless task. Mr. Williams, at the close of the nomination proceed- ings, delivered a short speech at the Swansea Liberal Club, and met with an enthusiastic reception. The new Liberal M.P. is said to be the largest tinplate manu- facturer in the world. His life story is one of the romances of industrial progress. Forty years ago he was employed as a lad in the Upper Forest Steel and Tinplate Works, at Aforriston, of which he is now pro- prietor. Whilst engaged in the mills as a "cold roll" boy he met with an accident which led to the amputa- tion of his left leg. On recovery from this accident, which had incapacitated him for his old employment, a place was found fur him in the counting-house. The young man showed marked aptitude for business, and passing through successive gradations, he secured in 1868 a position as manager of the Swansea Tinplate Works, then owned by Sir John Jenkins, who was spoken of as a Dissentient Liberal candidate for the recent vacancy in the Swansea district. Shortly afterwards , Mr. Williams started business himself in the tinplate ' trade. He was phenomenally successful, and bore a considerable part in the development of the great Welsh , industry. To-day the poor working lad of a few decades ago is one of the largest and most respected employers of labour in South %Vale. He is sole pro- prietor and manager of the Upper Forest Tinphte Works, Morriston Tinplate Works, and the Morlais Tin- plate Works—factories which find daily employment for over 2500 men and boys. The new member is a Noncon- formist of a stalwart type, being attached to the Welsh Congregationalists. His political creed is robustly Liberal, and he is a warm admirer of Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Williams is a magistrate for the Borough of Swan- I sea, and also for the county of Glamorgan. He has acted as mayor of Swansea, as a membsr of the , Glamorgan County Council, and as deputy chairman of the Glamorganshire Banking Company. He was born in 1840, and is therefore in his 53rd year. Mr. Williams, who is a fluent speaker in English and Welsh, will prove a valuable accession to the Welsh Parliamentary party

div.head: DARKWOOD.
div.p: DARKWOOD.
A TALE OF LONEMOOR.
BSI Mn. UARRIET LEWIS, Author of "Her Double pfe," " Old Life's Shadows," "Lady Kildare," eta.
CHAPTER. XLI. WILL snE ACCEPT HIM?

The clock (lin-led the hour of midnight before Miss Norreys stirred from her rapt attitude before the fire, and before she touched the bell at her elbow and summoned Nays. The East Indian glided in her soft flowing robes of unstiffened silk, and laid out her mistress's night robe. Miss Norreys exchanged her evening dress for a white cashmere wrapper trimmed with swansdown, and resumed, her seat, wifile Naya opened a large ebony dressing case, heavily bound in silver, and brought out Crushes and combs mounted in ivory, and ornamented with monograms in silver. While she brushed out the long silken lengths of dusky brown hair she furtively glanced now and then at the pale, olive face, with its thoughtful look, and noted how white were the usually seaclet lips and what dusky shadows lay underneath' the great brown eyes. " Mis,sy is not well to-night,' she said, softly, "Missylis tired with all this excitemeasof accident and visitors." " Yes, I am tired, Naya," said Miss Norreys, wearily. "How is your patient to-night ?" "She is sleeping like a baby, missy," answered Nays. "She has wakened only once this after- noon. The doctor came in again to see her, but he said that she was doing well. "I will look in upon her presently," said the lady. "How your touch soothes me, Nays. My head throbs in esery part to-night." The maid brushed gently and continuously in silence. When she had finished, and had coiled the dusky masses in a-earonal around. Miss Norrey's head, the latter arose, saying— " Lay out my night-things, Naya, while I look in upon your patient." She passed into the inner room, while her atten- dant obeyed her bidding. The light was turned low in the bedchamber. Its soft mellow rays fell upon the low brass bed- stead and the girl, who was enclosed in those soft falling curtains of white lace and rose silk. Miss Norreys stood by the bedside and looked down upon the sleeper. The girl's hair of bronze. gold streamed in massive waves over the lace- trimmed pillow. Her pure face, Greek in its out- line, sweet and lovely as an angel's vision, was calm in its repose. The pansy-dark eyes were thinly veiled by the transparent lids. The thin red lips wore slightly parted. Her night-robe, which belonged to Miss Norreys, was unbuttoned at the throat, and the lace frill fell away from the slender throat and milk-white neck. How beautiful she was. Yet even in her sleep a look of weariness was upon the young face—the shadow of a groat trouble hung over her. Miss Norreys looked upon her first in admiration then in tenderness. She knelt down beside the bed and studied Gwen's face feature by feature. And an infinite yearning filled the lady's soul for this tender young creature with the shadow of sor- row-upon her. " She, too, has suffered, and she is but a child I" she thought. "An orphan, doubtless ; poor, of course ; a hired companion in Lord Dark-wood's heme L-a companion to that vulgar overgrown girl I Poor child." She stooped and kissed Gwen with a tenderness such as none but Gwen's lover had ever exhibited to her before. _ . . .

I must keep her as long as I can," thought Miss Norreys." Matters have turned out differ- ently from my expectations. I will not abandon my new home. I shall not be able to withdraw myself from Lord Darkwood's visits-even if I wauld. I will fill my house with company. I will invite young people. I will interest myself in others. Else shall go mad with these haunting memories ! I must forget myself in making others happy." She knelt long at the bedside, and finallgreturned to her tjressing-room, where a bed had been pre- pafred for her. " Nays," said her mistress, suddenly, " I think I! soil fill Beechmont with visitors. 1 begiii to tire ! already of its solitude. I might go up td--London ' for the remainder of the season, but I am in no humour for town gaieties." " Who would come at this seaton, missy 1" asked the East Indian.

"Very many people with whom I became ac- quainted during my stay in town, besides others whom I have long known," answered Miss Norreys. "here is Mrs. General Kenright, under whose escort I came from India nearly a year ago. She is still'in England, and would be delighted to visit me. She knew papa, too, and that would be a link between us. And there are her daughters, Miss Kenright and Miss Emily, both delightful girls. And there is Colonel Warburton, who accompanied us from India. He has changed into a home regi- ment, and doesn't care a fig for the London season. Besides, I fancy that he is more than half in love with Miss Kenright, nd iI he had a chance would ask her to marry him. And there are two acquaint- ances I made in London, Miss Ensor, and her brother, Sir William Ensor, who are very agree- able, and who would gladly become members of my party. A,ld last of all there is Lord Chilton. I met him often in town, and, although Parliament is in session, I know he could come also."

Naya smiled. Lord Chilton is very handsome, missy, ells suggested. " I wishl he would come." "Ho is younger than I," said Miss Norreys. "I like him as a brother, and he would make a very pleasant cavalier for Miss Emily Kenright or for Miss Ensor." _ - .

"I wish, missy," said the East Indian with un- wonted energy, "that you would think of yourself sometimes, instead of always thinking of others. Why don't you have a title and husband to adore you!" A cloud settled heavily upon Miss Norresos brow. "I shall never marry, Nays," she declared. "Never speak to Inc again of marriage. I hate mankind, I often think. At any rate, the man does not live whom I would marry." " You wouldn't marry this Lord Chilton, then V' "No. He is little more than a boy, Naya. He has reeently come into his title and property through the death of his father. I saw much of him in London, and he has made me his confidante. He loYes some one else,, Naya, some young girl in Yorkshire or London, and whom be has in some seal lost, He has sought everywhere for her, but. in vain. But even if he loved me, I should but smile at his folly; Naya. My heart is dead within me. I have lost all power of loving," Naya shook her head. She did not quite believe this statement, although she knew it to he made in sincerity. Miss Norreys was too warm-hearted and noble to live all her life alone, the woman thought. She knew how desolate was that life Miss Norreys now lived. She knew what nights of anguish Miss Norreys now endured, and What a void reigned in her aching heart: The mistress disrobed and went to bed. Nays shaded the light softly, and went out to her own chamber, which adjoined the bedroom Gwen now occupied. Miss Norreys tossed .long upon her pillow, with that one thought and that one imagine possessing her mind—the thought and image ef Lord Dark- wood.. The next day Owen was better, and was up add dressed, her box having been sent with that of the Lady Georgina. She wore her arm in a sling, and did not venture to leave Miss Norrey's private apartments, perfect quiet and seclusion being deemed necessary for her. She lay all day on a couch, and .Naya served her, and Miss .Norreys read to her and petted her, and Owen was strangely happy. Her heart had gone forth to her beautiful hostess in an enthusiastic love such as young girls often felt for others of their sex. Miss Norreys seemed to her the incarnation of Leauuy, goodness, and nobleness, and she bestowed upon her an enthusi- astic worship such as she had never felt before for anyone.

And Miss Norreys, touched by her admiration and adoration, felt for her a yearning tenderness that was as new as strange. " They are already as loving as two -sisters," thought Naya, delightedly, lovin her mistress too well to entertain a spark 'of jealousy. "Missy ought to keep, this gird wi.th her.- She ought not to let her go back to..oii_nitelin Castle. She might, be missy's companion, and Lc petted and loved to her heart's content. - Missy wants a plaything like this girl." -- Perhaps Miss ,Norreys VI-ought so 00, for she devoted herself to GWO bpon this (lay; said the Lady Georgina, conceiving herself injured by these attentions to her companion, sulked and sat apart for hours, making herself dbeidedlv disaarLeable.

Lord Dark woed called upon this day also to inquire after Miss Myner. He saw Miss Norreys, had an interview with her, and went away, his in- fatuation deepened and strengthened into a great passion. Ho had no suspicion that he had ever seen Miss Norreys before, but he was resolved to make her his wife. _ _
This had already become the leading purpose of his life his one ambition—his great and fixed &termination. .

She was rich, of excellent family, of wonderful beauty. She met in full all his requirements. She satisfied his reason and his heart, His will: which had swept an open path before him nearly always, was bent upon the accomplishment of his design. And Miss Norreys read his purpose in his admir- ing glances, his softened tones, his very attitude. After he had gone she thought— "He loves me. He intends to ask me to be his wife. I have said that I should never marry, yet if he asks me to marry him, perhaps I may. And therein will lie my revenge. I almost think that I will marry him." She pondered the question often throughout that day and during the days that followed. During that day also she wrote out the invita- tions she had designed sending, and dispatched them to their several addressee. Gwen's stay at Beechdont was prolonged for a week, it not being-fleemed advisable for her to return to Dunholni Castle sooner, .

Her recovery under the care the received was rapid. The lady Georgina was for the most part goodnatured, and enjoyeclisher visit. The friend- ship between Miss Norrevs and Gwen deepensed with every day and hour, but the former made no attempt to win the girl into her service as coin- passion. Lord Darkwood called at Beechmont every day. His devotion had become patent to the Beechmont household, to the Dunholm Castle retainers, and even to the Lady Georgina, who was quite unrecon- ciled to the idea of her father's second marriage. The marquis desired the two girls to remain at Beechmont as long as possible, in order to afford excuse for his daily visits to Miss Norreys ; but that lady graciously informed him that she expected visitors, and invited him to come often during their stay, saying that also should depend upon him to assist in the entertainment. _ _

At the end of the week, Georgina and Gwen' now herself again, returned to Dunholm Castle. Before. they quitted Beechmont, letters had been received from the various persons invited, accepting Miss Norreys's invitation, and the guests were expected to arrive during the following week. Gwen had heard that Lord Chilton would visit Beeclanont, and her heart thrilled at the sound of that name. She believed Lord Chilton to be the father of her lover, Ronald Chilton, whom she deemed false to her, and she longed to see him, herself miknown.
" Ronald will not be here;" she said to herself. "It is well. . I could not bear to look upon his face again." And yet Ronald, her lover, was the Lord Chilton who was to arrive at Beechmont. _ _ _
Would they meet? And, If so, what would come of that Meeting ?
CHAPTER XLII.
THE GUESTS AT BEECHMONT.

The expected guests of Miss Norreys arrived in due course dt Beechmont, and a round of gaieties was inaugurated. First came Mrs. Gerald Kenright and her two daughters. The mother was a short, stout, full- blown dame, with a ribicund visage, on which sat a kindly expression. In spite qf her lack of beauty she was a Charming lady, gentle and soft-voiced, and motherly. She was very fond of Miss Norreys. ghe had chaperoned her during a number of years in India, and had been a most intimate friend of the Norreys Miss Kenrith was a,tall, gaunt lady of twenty- seven, pleasant and witty. She was reputed a blue, could discourse upon art by the hour, quoted Rus- kin continually, and wa.s, perhaps, more calculated to win admiration than love. Miss Emily, or as she was usually called, Miss Milly Kenriglit, was four years younger than her sister, an airy blonde, pretty, soft, and caressing, with no great strength of character, but with a fund of spirits that made her the life of any small pleasure party. The day after the arrival of the Kenrights came Colonel Warburton, Miss Kenright's especial ' admirer.

He was a portly man, bald, fine-looking, with long side whiskers. He had been a lover of Miss Norreys in India, and only after repeated rejec- tions had transferred his attentions to Miss Nor- reys's friend. By a later train upon the same day with the last- named arrival came Sir William Ensor and his sister. The former was a type of the ordinary British young gentleman, well-bred, good-tem- pered, and indolent, excellent company-in a coun- try house. The latter was a gay, frolicsome girl of twenty, devoted to out-door sports, fond of riding to hounds in the season, and fond of croquet, tennis, and other out-door games. Out of these different and seemingly incongrous materials, a most delightful family party was con- structed. Mrs, Kenrith matronised the young people, and all was gaiety and pleasure. Lord Chilton appeared a day later than 'the other guests. He was a handsome, noble looking young gentleman of five and twenty fair of face, with keen blue eyes—but why should we describe him? Our readers know that Lord Chilton, newly come into his title, was no other than our old friend Ronald Chilton, Gwen's lover, who had wooed her on the wild Yorkshire moors, won her love, and, as she believed, had thought better of his proposal of marriage, and had left her. He had spent month's searching for Gwen. He had visited every quarter of London, had travelled over England, had even gone upon the Continent to look for her, lie ha..(l employed skilled assist- ants in the search, had advertised in the news- papers in a manlier which she alone might under- stand; but all his efforts had failed. No trace could be found of the beautiful girl who had gone up to London alone to seek her fortune. She seemed to have disappeared utterly from among the living. Lord Chilton had visited Lonemoor repeatedly during the winter, offering the Quillets handsome bribes if they would reveal to him Gwen's address, but they had absolutely refused. He had implored them to do so, employing every argument that was likely to move. them, but all to no purpose. They were deg alike to his premises and entreaties. They wereconscientious, in their way ; they deemed Gwen a very unsuitable match for him, and they would not countenance his attentions to her. They had made up their minds that Gwen must continue single throughout her life, and they deemed their opinion infallible. So each time Lord Chilton came away from Lone. moor disheartened, having only for consolation the conviction that Gwen was not (lead, for, if she had been dead, would not the Quillets have known of ! ber death and have told him ? _

He had but recently heard of Squire Markham's return home after his years of wanderings, and the idea had come to him to see the old squire and interest him in his love story. Squire Markham must have unbounded influence over his old ser- vants. and at his command they would reveal to the lover the secret of Gwen's whereabouts. This idea was very strong in the young viscount's mind when he came to Beecinnont.

What had caused him to accept Miss Norreys's invitation he scarcely knew himself. He was not in a mood for visiting or. pleasure. making. He had met Miss Norreys in London at the house of a noble lady, to whom the East India heiress had brought letters of introduction. General Norreys had been a friend of his late father, and Miss Norreys had brought a letter to the late Lord Chilton, which, as he was dead, shelled delivered to the son. Ho admired the beautiful brunette greatly. He was charmed by her graciousness and sweetness; but even she had ndt Power to win his allegiance, had she so desired, from lovely, lost Gwen.

Re was tempted sometimes in the warmth and brightness of Miss Norreys's presence to tell her all about Gwen; but he felt that he could not do so in honour—that his lips were sealed. The strange mystery of Gwen' origin—that dishonourable grave at Penistone—alt, he could not speak of these even to Miss Norreys. Ile hoped to find Gwen, to make her his wife, and he hoped to see these two dear friends some day. Not for worlds then would he prejudice Miss Norreys against his betrothed. "She cannot know how peerless my Gwen is," he thought. "And if she knew of that cloud upon my &trial:es history she m;ght think ill things of her. Gwen is a lady in every instinct, and Miss, Norreys must meet her on equal ground to appre- ciate her. My poor little Gwen I What must she think of me 9"
The thought was anguish to him. Ile was. thin and worn by the winter's.unavailing search and anxieties, and he decided to visit Beech- mont for diversion from his hanntina sorrows and.

the regrets that consumed his sou!. But it was fate or Providence that brought him there. That Providence which had all her life guarded and guided the friendless girl was still watchful and beneficent, and was working gradually to bring about the reunion of the lovers: With the appearance of Lord Chilton, Miss Nor- reys's party was complete. The Month was April, the weather unusually settled and pleasant. Spring had set in early, with soft breezes, balmy skies, and delicious sunshine. The country roads were in excellent order, the Beechmont gardens bright with flowers and leafage, the well-drained lawns, smooili as velvet, level and eoftly-tinted. Every requisite for enjoyment was offered the fortunate guests. Miss Norrey's stables were filled with magnificent specimens of horseflesh. There were carriages of every kind, even to a Bath chair for Mrs. Kenright, when that lady, by reason of obesity, felt unable to walk about the grounds. Every kind of amusement that would be likely to interest young ladies and gentlemen was devised. Croquet parties out of doors were in blgh vogue. Archery was practised, and the young ladies exhibited considerable proficiency in the use of bow and arrow.

Lord Chilton felt out of place amid all this bright- ness and merry-making. He regretted his coming ; but since he was there, he made the best of it, was courteous and thoughtful of others about himseif being a gentleman—and endeavoured to contribute his share to the general enjoyment. But what hard work it was, only Miss Norreys could guess.

She knew that ho had experienced some dis- appointment in love. He had told her once, in a moment of despondency and craving for sympathy, when in London, that he had loved and lost a peer- less girl, who still lived, but whose whereabouts he did not know • but be had said no more. The pretty Miss Mily and the frolicsome Miss Ensor were alike powerless to win an admiring look from his lordship, yet he was kind and courteous to them as to the rest. The opinion prevailed among Lord Chilton's fellow guests that he was "not a marry- ing man." Lord Darkwood, accompanied by his daughter, made a prompt visit of ceremony to the llcechmont guests. Gwen was left at home, partly because she was not sufficiently recovered from her recent acci- dent to bear fatigue, and partly because the Lady Georgina, realising her own lack of beauty; did not choose to be overshadowed by her lovely young companion. . . . „

The marquis and his daughter had a fioece con- flict over the matter that morning in the library before setting out upon their visit. Georgina was fond of Gwen, but she was far snore fond of herself. She declared that Miss Norreys had'pitid snore attention to Gwen than to her during their recent stay at Beechmont, and that she would not submit to be cast into the background by her own hired companion. She would go without Gwen, or she would not go at all. Gwen was summoned to the excited conference, listened to Georgina's declara- tions, and then quietly declared her inability to accompany her charge by reason of her still dis- abled arm.

She. did not seemed to be wounded by Georgina's unfeeling words and manner. Poor Gwen was used to slights by this time, and was too proud to show that she even noticed them. But it was quite pos.. Obi() that in her own room the lonely young com- panion broke down sometimes in her cool hauteur, and sited tears over her unpleasant lot. Even a meek and patient Grillelda would have found it very hard to bear. sball 5t go with me to-day," cried Qesrginia, jealously, • nor shall she be present when they come here. F won't be cast into shadow by a hired companion. Mrs. Dover is a lady, and if a sheep dog is necessary when people call upon me, let her be sheep dog. Why, Marian is not much over a year older thau I. She is not suitable for a duenna. She needi & duenna as muck as I."

Lord Daftwood finally assented to his daughter's demands, the more readily that he secretly chafed at the strong contrast between his daughter and his daughter's governess. It wounded his pride that the hired companion should look so thoroughly "the lady of high degree," while his daughter might have passed for Gwen's maid, lloegan to give his daughter credit for more perception and sense than he had supposed her to possess, and to think it best that the two girls should not appear in society together. "I would not have Permitted Georgina to leave her schoolroom for even one visit," he thought, "but that I deemed her companionship a benefit during my first call upon Miss Norreys. Now that Georgina has become intimate at Beechmont, she will have to visit there while Miss Norreys guests remairy Afterwards, she will return to the school- rosm.r Miss Myner must, as Georgina says, keep in the background. The Lady Georgina passed through the ordeal of the visit with unexpected credit. She had developed an intense pride in her rank and pro- spective grandeurs, and carried herself very well, being rather silent and yet not at all abashe(L She wore a visiting dress of pale blue silk, a white cashmere jacket, heavily embroidered, and a white chip hat trimmed with tulle and blue forget-me- note. Due consideration had been paid to her youth in the design of this costume, and it was very becoming to her vague complexion and hay. coloured hair. Under her weight of finery she sat very conscious, never forgetting for one moment that she was the lady of highest rank present, and should, therefore, although yonngest, take prem. deuce of all the rest.

Miab Norreys inquired kindly after Miss Myner, and expressed her regrets on hearing that she was not yet frilly recovered. "I will come and see her to-morrow," said the lady. "I admire Miss Myner excessively. She is. as lovely as she is beautiful. lam sorry that she could not come with you." "We regretted it very much," said Lord Dark. wood. "Visa Myner is very fortunate in having won your favour, Miss Norreys." Lord Chilton wai sitting near, and listened idly to the conversation. If lie had only known who was this "Miss Mynor " of whom they talked But while he listened, his thoughts were busy with a letter he had decided to write to Squire Mark- ham. Why should he go to Lonemoor, when he could write to the old squire and present the case in better terms than he could do in words ! He determined to write that very day—as soon as these guests should depart. Miss Norreys invited Lord Darkwood and his daughter to remain to luncheon, and they accepted the invitation,

At the table, the conversation turned upon Dun' holm Castle, the antiquity of the portion now in ruins, the legends connected with it, and Colonel Warburton expressed a desirobto explore the ruins. " A grand idea !" exclaimed Miss Ensor. "We will all go. Miss Kenright adores antiquities, and she will study the stone walls and buttresses ana tell us the very year they were founded. And for us inferior mortals--Miss Milly and I—there will be a picnic in the old banqueting-hall and a dance afterwards. Lord Darkwood, you may prepare for an_invasion."

Lord Darkwood changed colour. An uneasy gleam appeared in his crafty eyes. He was about to allege that the floors were insecure, and that he had therefore refused longer to admit visitors to the ruins, when the Lady Georgina cried Vivaciously— "Oh, you must all come ! When there are a number of people one needn't be afraid, and those old rooms are so strange and delightful. I've been . all through them, even to the dungeons. And we heard a horible sound in the•clungeons just like a groan or shriek, you know, and it made our very flesh creep." Lord Darkwood frowned upon his daughter, but she, absorbed in self, was oblivious of hina. " GeorgirD. heard an owl," he said, explainingly, forcing a siiTile. "She is a perfect coward, fright- ened at a sound !" •

"Oh, but 4at was terrible !" cried the Lady Georgina with a shudder. "Even Marian, my companion, was frightened, and she is brave as one of the Six Hundred—Tennyson's Six Hundred you know, in thc poem. I thought it was the ghost." "Has Dunholm Castle a ghost?" asked Miss Kenright, smiling. " Beeehmont lacks nothing but a ghost. Does your family spectre reveal him- self to visitors, Lord Darkwood ?" „

"No," answered the marqui—s.. "Our spectre is a creature of the servants' imaginations. The ruins have not been shown for several months, and arc not considered in excellent repair. I should hesitate to invite so large a party when the place is possibly insecure—" "Oh, father," interzupted Georgina, "there were large picnic parties in the ruins very often last summer. Mrs. Dover told me so; and they had dances by moonlight, and all that sort of thing. And Mrs. Dover says that she thinks your shutting up the ruins to be an excess of precaution,' and that it isn't at all necessary." If Lord Darkwood could at that moment have immured his daughter in a convent for the term of her natural life, he would have done it cheerfully. VA haled her with an unreasoning hatred. He felt

that he could strike her down before ms eyes. Yet he was obliged to assume a smile and look com- placently, even while his eyes stared at her angrily. Miss Norreys marked the expression of his es'ee and wondered greatly thereat. She comprehended that the marquis did not desire visitors at the ruins. Visitors had alwaYe been allowed there. Why had he changed the old custom? She pondered these questions, and was very thoughtful. "We will all be guided by the opinion of Mrs - Dover," said Miss Ensor, gaily. "The floors are secure enough for us, Lord Darkwood. We shall certainly pay you a visit, and hunt out your ghost' owl, and dance by moonlight in the old banquetieg Miss Milly Kenrig'a eagerly seconded the baronet's sister, and Sir William Ensor joined in gaily. The matter appeared settled. Nothing remained for the marquis but to submit with aa good grace as posssble ; but a cold sweat sprang out. of his forehead, and his complexion had a siol4 hue, as he exclaimed— "lf you decline my advice, and will take the responsibility, I will make you welcome at Dunholin Castle at any time you may appoint. But allow me to make one or two suggestions. * Instead of a Pic" nic I shall be happy to provide you with a suitable, collation. We shall have moonlight evenings' next week, and your (lance will then be in orders Let us appoint Wednesday of next week the daY of your visit and explorations." Mrs. Kenright made some faint demur to his lordship's trouble in the matter, and Miss Norreye begged to be allowed to make the affair a picnic ) but the marquis, who had now recovered his self- possession, would not consent to change his pleat and Miss .Norreys and her guests accepted the invi- tation to dine at Duuhohn Castle on the ensuing Wednesday. Shortly afterwards Lord Darkwood and the Lady Georgina went home. During the drive the marquis was perfectly silent, havini, due regard to the footmen; but, when he entered ° the castle, he conducted his daughter to the library, and there he expounded to her the enormity of her conduct, condemned her impertinence and officiousness, eed threatened that, if it were repeated' he would send her to a French convent.' Then he dismissed her, and sat down to grapple with certain problems of great intricacy that presented themselves to hie mind. As soon as Lord Darkwood had withdrawn with his daughter from Beechmont, Miss Norreys sent a messenger to her bailiff, Mr. Barnsby, who resided in a pretty villa at Dunhohn village, requesting his immediate presence at Beechmont. Mr Barnsby was a shrewd, elderly man, honbst. keen-witted, and clear headed, who had been recommended to Miss Norreys by her Londe° solicitor as land agent, bailiff and general over' looker and manager of her estate. Miss Norreye regarded him as perfectly trustworthy, which indeed he was, and as devoted to her interests, which was also true. He obeyed her summons and was shown her private boudoir, where she awaited him - Their interview was prolonged for hours. And, at the conclusion of that interview—which Nra9 destined to prove very important in its ultimate results—Mr. Barnsby returned home in hot haste, packed a carpet-bag, and departed for Shrewsburh, whence he took tho night express for London. (To be continued.) 7P' ;

div.head: FACES OF GREAT MEN..
div.p: THE FACES OF GREAT MEN..

Four faces among the portraits of modern tiletrt' great or small, strike us as supremely beautiful, 11?„ merely in expression, but in the form and proP tion and harmony of features—Shakspere, Rafft`er, Gcethe, and Burns. One would expect it to be s°,.; for the mind makes the body, not the body tn` mind ; and the inward beauty seldom fails to ex:' press itself in the outward, as a visible sign of tb6t invisible grace or disgrace ot the wearer. Not tha it is so always. A Paul, apostle of the Gentilesil may be ordained to be 'in presence weak,in sPesch contemptible," hanapered by some thorn in the Iles —to interfere with the success of his mission, Reri; haps for the same wise purpose of Providence wille f sent Socrates to the Athenians, the worshippers °D physical beauty,in the ugliest of human bedies,thaa they, or rather those of them to whom eves to se had been given, might learn that soul is after !11l ,e independent of matter, and not its creature and i" slave. But, in the generality of cases physiognottl,Y is a sound and faithful science, and tells lig, if Ilf,;; alas ! what the man might have been, still what he .h 5 become. Yet even this former problem, what he have been, may often be solved for us by youthfuA portraits, before sin and sorrow and weakness have ba' their will upon the features ; and, therefore, when urei spoke of these four beautiful faces, we alluded, in eact case, to the earliest portraits of each genius which could recollect. Placing them side by side, we must I). allowed to demand for that of Robert Burns an honour; able station among them. Of ShaltSPere's we do ncy speak, for it seems to us to combine in itself the elan° of all the other three ; but of the rest we questioir; whether Robert Burns's be or not, after all. ~ke net the noblest, still the most lovable—the moat what we should wish that of a teacher of men to 13%,. Raffirelle—the most striking portrait of him, perhaps., /1„ the full-face pencil sketch by his own hand in the TaPc„, Gallery in Oxford—though without a taint of littlenef: or effieminacy, is soft, melancholy, formed entirely receive and to elaborate in silence. Dis is a face to D° kissed,not worshipped. Geethe, even in his earliest porr; traits, looks as if his expression depended too much his own will. There is a self-conscious power, pose, and self-restraint, and all but scorn, upon glorious lineaments, which might win worship, and di" but not love, except as the child of enthusiasm or of rr- lationship. But Burns's face, to judge of it by the ea,rl,llo portrait of him by Nastnyth, must have been a race that of Joseph of old, of whom the rabbis relate, that 061 was mobbed by the Egyptian ladies whenever he walk the streets. The magic of that countenance, makil Burns at once tempter and tempted, may explain trls,rif a Fad story. Mr. Andrew Carnegie, the American "Iron King," who on Monday started with Mrs. Carnegie and a party of private friends on a coaching tour through England and Scotland, has returned to his old love in the matter of the Scottish seat which he has taken for the season. Last year he spent the summer at Glen Bannock, Perthshire. This year he once more rents Cluny Castle, Inverness-shire, from the Cluny Macphersons. Me considers the scenery of Speyside superior to that ot the Perth- shire Highlands. Along with Cluny Castle he has taken, for the accommodation of his visitors, Craig- dliu House. This is situated about two miles from Cluny Castle, on the banks of Loch Ovie, and at the foot of Craig-dhu, or the Black Craig, within the rocky recesses of which Prince Charlie took refuge after the Battle of Culloden. Mr. Carnegie states that Mr. John Morley once described Craig-dhu House as an ideal Highland residence. It belonged to Mrs. Fitzroy, a sister of Cluny Mac- pherson.

The Carnegie coaching party intend visiting the valley of the Wye, and driving through the Western counties of England on their way north, On a previous occasion some years ago, when Mr. Car- negie made a coaching tour through the island, he published a very pleasantly written book about it, and we shall probably have from his pen a similar account of the present cruise on wheels.

div.head: FRAUDULENT LETTER SORTERS VISIT
div.p: FRAUDULENT LETTER SORTERS VISIT
WARRINGTON.

At Bury Police Court, on Friday, James Earn- shaw and W. T. Jackson, sorters at Stalybridge, were again brought up for being concerned in a series of frauds on the post office. Mr. Elliott said Earnshaw was charged with having, on March 16, at Stalybridge, forged and uttered a Savings Bank deposit book for payment of £5O with intent to defraud; with,on the 29th March, forging and alter- ing an order for the payment of £3O; with forging another order for 3s. ; with feloniously uttering and disposing of the altered bank book referred to. Jackson was charged with aiding and abetting in the committal of the felonies. He intended to deal with the two cases as one, and then ask the bench to commit the prisoners for trial on a charge of conspiracy. On th 3 18th March last a man went to the Winwick-st.,post office, Warring- ton, and got a deposit book, in the name of Eli Lee, Widnes, paying in ss. The year was not put in, but 1892 had since been put, the date stamp altered, the ss. altered to £7 54. and further entries of £22 15s. in October last and £2O in January last as of deposits being made on those dates being found in the book. Both entries were fictitious, as also were the date stamps. The Hyde clerk would swear the writing of his initials was that of Earnshaw. In March a letter was received in London for the withdrawal of three of the five shillings deposited by Lee at Warrington with a request that the money should be raid at Man- , chester. This was done. The place of payment was, however, altered from Manchester to Manchester-road, Warrington,. and a fictitious advice note was got and altered from 3s. to £44 3s. This advice note was sent under cover,an unusual thing,and excited suspicion, and the postmistress at Warrington refused to pay the money, which had been asked for in £lO money orders. When Earnshaw was arrested at Bury, Detective Brooks found upon him the deposit book, the warrant for four money orders at £lO each, a sheet of paper naming the £44 35., Sze. When asked who had signed the warrants Earn- shaw said "I did." Annie Wood, of Winwick-st. Post Office, bore out Mr. Elliott's statement as to issuing the bank book in March last, and as to the alteration of the date stamp and the figures. Abraham Hall, of Hyde Post Office, said the sums entered in the deposit book as paid at Hyde were never paid there, and his initials were forgeries. Some of the alterations were in Earn- shaw's writing, but he could not see any in Jackson's. Both prisoners knew witness's writing. A clerk from London proved the forgery of the withdrawal advice note and its alteration. Mrs. Jordan, sub-postmistress at Manchester-road office, Warrington, deposed that the prisoner E trnshaw gave his notice ter withdraw the £4O in money orders, and two days after his brother,Harold Earnshaw, came for the money, but she refused to pay it, as there were several suspicious circumstances about the case.—Evidence as to Earnshaw's arrest and that the bank book for £43 35., a savings bank warrant for £44, and notice of withdraw' of 3s. were found upon him, was given, and that he admitted signing the war- rants. Nothing, however was found in Jackson's houso or on him connected with these cases. Earnshaw was committed for trial on this charge, but the bench de- clined to commit Jackson, against whom they held that nothing had been said although Mr. Elliott asked that he should be committed on general conspiracy.—Bail was refused.
LABOUR ELECTORAL ASSOCIATION.

The sixth annual Conference of the Labour Electoral Association was opened on Monday, at Hull, Mr. W. Bailey of the Nottinghamshire Miners' Association,being in the chair. In his opening address Mr. Bailey spoke of the ephemeral character ef some rival associations, and said that the Labour Electoral Association had a solid basis of trade-union membership. It had made gosd progress, which wobld have been still greater but for the policy pursued by the Independent Labour Party. Real labour work was checked and the interests of the workers damaged by the action of that party. The Labour Electoral Association would continue its policy of seeking to construct rather than destroy—to build rather than pull down. The thanks of the Conference were given to the President far his address, after which the annual report of the Association was presented by Mr. Threlfall, the secretary, and adopted. The Labour Electoral Association, resumed its annual Conference on Tuesday at Hull, under the presidency of Mr. W. Bailey, of Nottingham. Much time was spent in discussing a resolution, moved by Councillor Robson, of Sheffield, asserting the paramount claims of labour and the necessity of active and determined efforts being made to secure the return to Parliament of a largely in- creased number of Labour members. In the course of the discussion the Independent Labour party came in fora good deal of criticism. Mr. Threlfoll said all at- tempts to associate Socialism with the Labour party must be resisted. An amendment which aimed at plac- ing the claims of labour above those of party politics was rejected, and the resslution was passed. A disous- sion aftnrwards took place on various items which, it was suggested, should be included in the programme of the Labour party. The sittings of the Labour Electoral Congress at Hull were brought to a close on Wednesday. During the day , resolutions were passed on a variety of questions. There I was a discussion of some interest on the Miners' Eight Hours Bill. Two delegates from the Durham miners opposed a resolution in favour of that measure. In Durham. they stated, the miners would work six hours a day. If the Bill passed they would probably be com- pelled to work longer. Mr. J. H. Wilson, M.P., and Mr. Harvey, of the Derbyshire miners, described this con- tention as absurd. Mr. Harvey spoke bitterly of the Durham system of giving the men six hours' work a day and the boys eight or mere hours, and of the payment of men by results and the boys by the day. The resolu- tion in favour of the Bill was passed. Mr. Sugden, of Bradfoiel. proposed a resolution urging the Government to give speedy effect to their Home Rule proposals. He held that the opposition to Home Rule was being pro- longed in the hope of delaying and defeating the demo- cratic measures included in the Government programme. The resolution was unanimously agreed

div.head: LIBERATOR SOCIETY.
div.p: THE LIBERATOR SOCIETY.

UNPROTECTED SHAREHOLDERS. Evidence with regard to the affairs of the Liberator Building Society was again given on Tuesday at the London Guildhall befare Mr. Registrar Emden. Mr. Thomas Davies, a chartered accountant and one of the directors' auditors, stated that securities were produced before him in respect of the Balfour group of compan- ies, but he did not satisfy himself whether they were first, second, or third mortgages. From large bundles of deeds " he took a bundle here and there," and so satisfied himself that they contained deeds and securities. He regarded it" as the duty of the directors to go into the value of the securities.' The Registrar during the examination of this witness remarked that the extra- ordinary evidence given in the course of the inquiry ought to have the effect of calling the attention of the Legislature to the absolute want of protection which shareholders in building societies laboured under in the matter of the management and audit of the accounts. There was absolutely no protection to shareholders of building societies in the way of audit. At the conclusion of Wednesday's proceedings in con- nection with the Liberator inquiry, the Registrar intim- ated that the inquiry must be adjourned sine the, and that all the witnesses whose evidence had not been fully concluded must be liable to be recalled until it could be ascertained whether the attendance of Mr. Walker and Mr. Jabez Balfour could not be secured.

div.head: IHE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 24; 1893. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IHE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 24; 1893. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY,
AYNUAL MEETING.

- - The annual meeting of the Warrington Musical Society was held on Monday evening at the Cairo- street schoolroom. Mr. John Ryiands (president) was in the chair, and there were present :—Mr. li. Atkin (secretary), Mr. W. E. Reynolds (treasurer). Mr.F. H. Crossley (conductor) ; Nlessra. D. Fetish aw, 11. Bond, J. Ne seeombe, G. Wallington, Price, J. Lee, R. Eccles, and others. THE SECRETARY'S REPORT. Mr. ATKIN, secretary, in presenting his report, first alluded to the unsatisfactory financial balance sheet that the Treasurer would submit that evening, still when they have heard his report bethought thay would agree, bearing in mind the disastrous conditions under which the last reason he'd passed, that the wonder was that they had not died. He expressed his pleasure, however, with being able to present a favourable report regarding the musical aims of the society. He hoped that it would serve as a sugar plum to counteract the nasty taste engendered by the balance being on the wrong side. The strength of the society in the first place called for approval. The numbers were :-83 sopranos 43 contraltos, 19 tenors, 28 basses, 30 members, making the strength of the chorus 151, and the mem- bership 181. Mr.Atkin then referred to the success of the two concerts that were held, and regretted the misfor- tune which prevented the taking place of the other two, I as was intended. Mr. Atkin then gave the number of re- hearsals that had beeit held during the past season,which amounted to 38. He regretted that he could not furnish I the average attendances at the Rehearsals owing to the carelessness of the members in not complying with the system that had been in force, viz ,by the marking of cards. The misappropriation of seats on the occasion of the Elijah concert was next commented upon. Mr. Atkin said that he offered his apologies to any subscri- bers who were subjected to the annoyance in question. The severe letter of " an old subscriber," which had ap- peared in the local papers illustrated the occurrence to which he referred in a slightly exaggerated form. He regretted, however, the coarse that the writer had pur- sued, because by hiding his identity he gave him (the secretary), no chance to personally apologise. He hoped that the feelings of the subscriber were not largely shared by others however. With that one exception, he thought that the Society had been admitted to have in no way offended during the past season. He reminded his hearers that the object of the Society was not to make money, but to give an intellectual pleasure and impart knowledge of music to its members, and if they had once again to plead poverty, he regretted it, but drew their attention to the fact that it had been the fate of many a honoured musical society. (Applause.) THE TREASURER'S REPORT. The TREASURER reported that the total receipts were £139 4s. 21., and the expenditure £lBl 95. 5d., leaving a deficit of £42 ss. 31. The Treasurer drew attention to the fact that although a number of subscribers had con- tributed towards four concerts, they did not demand the return of the overplus. There was only one exception, 'They gave the society the benefit of the Money, or took extra tickets in consideration of the money. Some people were good enough to pay the full subscription even when they were aware that the season had been halved. The statement and the Secretary's report were both adopted. THE PUBLIC HALL QUESTION, Sze. Mr. RYLANDS remarked that in view of the exceptional causes which had militated against their success, they might rest satisfied that their position was not worse. It was a regrettable position, however, and there was this feature about it, that they could not blame anyone. It was rather agreeable to be able to point out where a matter failed, and to be able to suggest a remedy, but in this case none could be blamed. The money would , have to be raised by some means. He had ne doubt that they would be able to raise it. They had always met deficiencies in the past. In the future he hoped that they would not have the expense of renting a hall,' for he understood that a public hall was on the eve of being built, which would be adapted for concerts. The plans he had seen were very promising, and he had no , doubt but that they would be carried out exactly as he I had seen them. The delay in the building operations had arisen from a variety of causes, the chief of which were difficulties in regard to the land. Then Mr. Parr had unfortunately been compelled to leave the town to recruit his health, and so operations were much delayed. He had no doubt that the building would be a handsome one, and he hoped that it would be available for concerts' is the course of a year or so. (Applause.) Mr. Rylands then moved a vote of thanks to the treasurer and secre- tary for their services, and this was agreed to with ac- clamation after being seconded by the Rev. F. Millard.— ' In returning thanks, Mr. Atkin referred to the valuable services rendered to the society by the conductor, Mr. F. H. Crossley, and Mr. Reynolds concurred in these re- marks.—Mr. WALLINGTON proposed that all the officers be re-elected. He remarked that they ought not to be discouraged because they had an adverse balance. He never knew any society which lied existed many years without getting into debt. He had no doubt that before long they would reduce it. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. LEE seconded, and it was decided upon the proposition of Mr. 11. BOND that Mr. Herbert Woods be placed on the committee in place of Mr. Tauranac.—Mr. NEWCOMBE proposed that a hearty vote of thanks be given to all those who had rendered valuable assistance during the past season, and especially ti Mrs. Edlesten, who in the last concert given, viz., " Athalie," had taken the part of reader with great success, and also Mrs. James Fair- dough, who had taken a great deal of trouble to make the concerts a success. They also had to thank those who did not ask for the return of subscriptions. Mr. Crossley, the conductor, who had worked so heartily and unceasingly, Mr. J. B. Caldwell, the organist, and Mrs. John Reynolds, who played during his absence.— Miss Werane seconded the resolution, which was heartily Carried.

MO:N DA Y. In the House of Commons on Monday evening Sir E. GREY, in answering a question as to the dispute between Franc, and Siam, said rue report of the despatch of a French fleet to Bangkok was not correct. In reply to Mr. F. Lockwood, Mr. MUNDELLA said he had t Limn the opinion of the law officers of the Crown on tim action of the Shipping Federation in the Hull dispute, and they had come to the conclusion that there had ben a technical infringement of the law. It was open to any person interested to prosecute, but the Board of Trade declined to make themselves in any way partisans in a trade dispute. But if the parties went beyond a technical infringement it would be his duty to pia se cute. The House again went into Committee on the Home Rule Bill, resuming consideration of clause 4. Several amendments were rejected, majorities ranging from 29 to 37. A lively discussion took place on an amend- tnent to deprive the Irish Legislature of the power te suspend the writ of habeas corpus. The further progress of the Rating of Machinery Bill and the Sacred Music on Sundays Bill was opposed, and discussion had to be postponed.

In the House of Lords two new peers—Lord Roberts and Lord Swansea—took their s2ats. The Earl of WIN- CHILSEA moved a resolution calling for legislation with a view to securing that the quantity of breadstuffs in the United Kingdom should never fall below a six months' supply. His Lordship spoke of the danger in this matter with which the country would be confronted in time of war. Lord PLAYFAIR, after referring to the groundlessness of the noble Lord's alarm, said that corn tnerchants informed him that such a socialistic scheme as he proposed would disjoint all the operations of the ordinary food supplies of the country. The motion was withdrawn. TUESDAY. In the House of Commons on Tucsday evening, Mr. ROBERTSON, replying to questions, said overtime had been permitted in the torpedo tube-shop at Keyham since November 1891, in order to complete the ship- building programtne under the Naval Defence Act ; but additional plant was now being procured, so that more men might be employed and overtime reduced. Mr. Gladstone was further interrogated about the desirableness of proclaiming a general holiday on the occasion of the Royal Wedding, and he repeated that he did not think an executive actign was called for.

Mr. FELLOWES moved the adjournment of the House in order to draw attention to " the persistent neglect of the Government "in the matter of swine fever. Mr. H. Gardner showed that the allegations in the motion were unfounded, and Sir W. HARCOURT asked whether the House was prepared to put another penny on the income tax. The motion was defeated by 285 to 252—majority for the Gwvernment 33.
The House then went into Committee again on the Rome Rule Bill, and several amendments were rejected by the customary majorities.
--- In the House of Lords the Places of Worship (Sites) Bill passed through Committee.
WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday, the House went into Committee on the Home Rule Bill, resuming consideration of clause 4, which sets forth that the Irish Legislature shall not have power to make certain laws. No fewer than twelve amendments standing in the name of Lord Carmarthen and other Conservative members were ruled out of order amid ministerial cheers. A lively debate took place on Mr. P. SrAith's amendment seeking to prevent the Irish Legislature from establish- ing a press censorship and from interfering with public meetings. Mr. John Morley and Mr. Sexton strongly condemned the Tory obstruction, and the latter said the amendment came from the party that had not only used press censorship as a main prop in Ireland for yeurs, but had shot innocent men at an admittedly legal meeting at Mitchelstown. The amendment was negatived without a division. Mr. D, PLUNICET proposed an amendment prohibiting the Irish Legislature from making any law affecting Trinity College, Dublin, or the Dublin Univer- sity. Mr. Gladstone showed that his fears were ground- less, and the amendment was rejected by a Government majority of 42. Another amendment similar in charac- ter was defeated. Progress was reported, and the House adjourned at a quarter to six o'clock.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday Mr. Farquhar- son brought up the Employers' Liability Bill as amended by the Standing Committee on Law. Mr. G. Russell informed Mr. Forwood that the opera- tion of the Indian load-line was temporarily suspended, pending the issue of new rules. Mr. Gladstone made a statement on the financial clauses of the Home Rule Bill. The Government pro- posed to establish what he might call a provisional term of six years for the financial arrangements, instead of a longer, term of fifteen years, capable of extension until interfered with. During these six years the plan would materially different. There would be no change pro- posed by the Government in fixing, managing, or collect- ing any of the taxes included in the present system of taxation. Secondly, there would be power given to Ireland to establish new taxes for herself. Ireland's contribution would be one third of her ascertained revenue, and also the whole yield of any taxes that might be imposed upon her by Parliament expressly for war or special defence. At the close of six years, such contributions and the financial particulars would be re- vised, and Ireland would collect, fix, and manage her own taxes, except the Customs. Excise, and the Post Office. Mr. John Redmond gave notice that he should oppose as unjust and humilating to Ireland the pro- posal to deprive the Irish Legislature of any control for six years over the taxation now being raised under Acts of Parliament. The House went into Committee on the Home Rule Bill, resuming the consideration of clause 4, and several amendments were dealt with.

EATON HALL.

Eaton Hall has, says the " World " been rebuilt by the Duke of Westminster at a total expense (including the elaborate and splendid internal decorations) of more than a million. It is an immense pile in the " Decor- ated " style, and it now rivals Chatsworth in popularity as a show place. Except during the winter series rf house-parties, the hall is uniahabited, for the " family- wing" practically forms a separate residence, and it is hero that the Duke and Duchess live when they are alone, and it affords ample accommodation for a small party. There are fine gardens at Elton, with a large park, and the wooded slopes towards the Dee are very pretty, but it does not take a high place among the picturesque country seats of England. The magnificent old house at Eaton, a masterpiece of Vanburgh, was pulled down about seventy years ago, and it was re placed by a structure which Mr. Greville described as "a vast pile of mongrel Gothic, which cost sonic hun- dreds of thousands, and it is a monument of wealth, ignorance, and bad taste." Eaton was the most am- bitious specimen of the debased Gothic which George IV. brought into fashion. The house abounded in mullioned windows, pointed arches, towers, turrets, pinnacles, battlements, and Gothic niches, with a pro- fusion of gilding. The library was copied from the lady-chapel of Salisbury Cathedral. The fastidious taste of the present duke was outraged by his grand- father's creation, and shortly after his accession he cleared away the whole building, and in the course of the next few years the present house was finished.

div.head: ST. HELENS MINERS AND NON-UNION
div.p: ST. HELENS MINERS AND NON-UNION
MEN.

- - In the House of Commons, on Thursday, Baron l. de Worms asked the Home Secretary whether his attention ,had been drawn to the circular issued to the miners in the St. Helens district by Mr. Thos.Glover, J.P., miners' agent, in which he said that having received power from the Lancashire Miners' Federation to force all non-union men into the union, the power being granted two months ago, and all the men not having yet joined, the St. Helens district had decided to give those men wbo were still out of the union until the 24th day of Jose to join; and if all had not joined by that date notice would he given to all where non-union men are employed for the purpose of stop- ping them ; and that all those who wero in the union and belonged to any other district must bring their cards of membership, as there would be men appointed to look at the cards once a month, and if any member was found "going bad "he would be warned of the same, and have to pay up at once ; whether he was advised that such threatening notices were legal, and if not, whether lie proposed to take any and what action in tie matter; and whether he was aware that these threatening notices were signed by Mr. Glover with the initials " J.P." after his name, lie having been recently appointed a borough magistrate. Mr. Asquith said his attention had been called to this circular. He was advised there was nothing illegal in its terms, and he did not propose to take any action in the matter. The circular in question was signed by Mr. Glover, but not with the initials •‘ J.P." affixed to his name. It appeared that in the case of a previous circu- lar Mr. Glover did append J.P." to his name. fie could not imagine that Mr. Glover was purporting to , act in a magisterial capacity. Mr. Glover thought and lie (Mr. Asquith) agreed with him, that in affixing his designation to such a document he made a mistake, which he assured him would not occur again. Baron H. De Worms : The previous circular was in the same terms as the one in question.—Mr. Asquith : It was not in the same terms.—lsaron H. De Worms :1 have it here.—Mr. Legh : Is Mr. Glover one of the recently appointed magistrates ?—No reply was given.
