div.head: WHITSUNTIDE FLIGHT
div.p: A WHITSUNTIDE FLIGHT
WITH THE WOODCOCK.
(BY Mn. JOHN PEERS )

The sun was shining brightly through every coign of vantage he could get in the awning and making fantastic patterns wherever his beams brighty fell, and had, doubtless, long been doing it, ere we were shamed into rousing and trying to prevent so glorious a morning from wasting its beauties unappreciated and unprofitably. Whit- Monday, 1893: surely this was one of the finest days of an exceptionally tine season. Bare legged and bare tooted out upon the cockle studded sand, intent upon making a raid upon these luscious bivalves. No need to travel far to get a boiling. The boat herself lay upon hundreds of them. The best ones are got by washing out of the steep sides of the "gores" or pools left by the tide. The best are then seen and can be selected. To free them from sand we hang them in a net over the stern when the tide is in. This gives them the opportunity of freeing themselves of the sand which is included in their hasty closing when rudely snatched from their native bed. A healthy cockle in situ pre- vents a heart-shaped appearance. There is one edge of this shell has a distinct cord tte appearance ; in health this is always uppermost and the "foot "down in the sand. This foot is an excellent digger. If a newly bared cockle is watched it will be seen to bury itself in a few seconds, providing the sand is sufficiently wet. But lo ! in the distance I see Tommy has raised a culinary smoke—happy presage of coffee and chops. Being in no mood to neglect the good the gods bestow, this promise of a sweet savour is effective. We realized, and then we were in a proper condition to appreciate the many glories of the ever to be remembered '93 Whit- Monday.

Plere, in the sunlit ozone laden air, it was one of those days in which to exist was a jay, and life itself a blessing. To those attuned by health and healthy in- stincts to its appreciation, such a day and such a place was full of delight. The gentle zephyr that fanned our cheeks served to temper the too fervid beams of a persistent sun. The warm sands were pleasant treading to the bare feet. The still air, unvexed by aught save sounds of nature—the peculiar "sweep "of the quilting cockle as he hastily closed his business premises on our approach—the curlew's cry for "Charlie Chorley "—or the shrill pipings of the " pars " as they wheel past flocked, in rapid flight. And very clear too is the at- mosphere ; distant things seem almost within touch. Yonder away to W. are the Ormes, little and great, with a detached hammock to the right which we know to be the Isle of the Puffin. Tracing back along the Welsh coast we have in prominence the Point of Air, with its red and white banded lighthouse, backed by the Flintshire Hills. The rest of the Welsh Dee coast is hid behind the nearer Hilbre Island, now, as the tide is out, an island only in name, but still the extreme N.W. extension of Cheshire, and a very picturesque addition to the landscape, con- spicuous by its rock-reds, its grass greens, and its well- whitened walls. Now this inconstant island—this geo- raphical paradox, which indulges in isolated hauteur Insular stand-offishness for eight out of a possible twenty four hours, while, by the irony of a cruel fate, it is com- pelled, for the remaining sixteen, to acknowledge its humbler connections of Lime Wharf and the tint shoals of the Cheshire shore.

As I have said this sometime island was to be our ' object this eve. At present we are hard and fast aground and the" island "is in the humbled stage of its daily changes. But after dinner we shall have the tide running up the" gutter," which divides our bank from the shore. At a place called the Red Rocks the tide from the Mersey meets the tide from the Dee. Here is the highest; and shoaliest part of the navigable channel through the Lake to Sabre, and is the watershed—the critical point—to get over which is an augury of the successful attainment of that destination. Slut the channel is winding and intricate at the watershed, los- ing itself in the indistinguishable flatness of the shoal. It is marked by two black buoys and a few bush- crowned perches. As the tides were low ones it was needful to know where the beet of it lay. Our pilot was sent over there to examine and take a few cross-bear- ings. He reported that the three perches in a line with the inner black buoy, upon reaching which this buoy keeps in line with the four houses on shore until the Beach Mark nearly aligned with the N. end of Hilbre houses, whence to S. end of Island leads clear. Taking an early start on the flood and following these sailing directions enabled us to scrape clear—after many scrapes —and bear away for the island—following in the wake of our old ship the " Doctor," now owned and located here. By this time the wind, having been light all day, now fell away altogether, entirely precluding any chance of going further westward as the tide was now near upon the point of ebb. But assuredly no great regret need be felt at having to make temporary lodgement here. For the evening was, and promised to be, a fitting end to so beautiful a day. Having found a berth—the anchor found and gripped the sandy bottom. And down through the unruffled surface and pellucid depths we could see the chain hanging in perpendicular idleness far below the boat; while the rudder and sharp fore-foot were plainly visible. Slowly and deliberately swung the boats in response to the ebbing tide, while we in response to the promptings of the stomachic ebb prepared and partook of Cowper' s cup. After which Tommy awakened mocking echoes from the rocks by vociferating—" Oh ! what a day we are going to have to-morrow !" to which piece of vocal anticipation he added the threat that his "Liberty he would regain." Now when one's chief mate takes a fit of this sort some- thing has to be done—something severe—for the repres- sion of mutinous insubordination. 'I he young rogue was ordered to be "marooned," so I rowed him ashore in the punt and turned him adrift upon that not quite desolate island. He did'nt seem to take this form of punishment much to heart,for, as heiscratubled over the slippery rocks towards the " Little Eye, he shocked the classic syrens of the Dee by jubilantly declaring that " Papa's on a tata by himself !" And so he made his way over the tide forsaken sands to West Kirby, from whence he returned what time the fitful moon gave uncertain leading to his steps across the splashing water- soaken sands.

Meanwhile, some visitors to the island who had trav- elled there in a broad wheeled cart, were laughingly loading up to return and, presently, away they went crunching over the rocky road until this, and their laughter laden voices, were lost in the distance, and then I was alone—they had " left the world to silence and to me." And, one by one, the stars came out and blinked benignly :on the scene below. So, while peace thus reigned in and around the boat, again the welcome shelter of the awning was sought, and enrugged and enwrapped,l slept the sleep of the just—abed. Responsive to the sailors " reveille "—the lap-lap of returning water and the shrill ./E dean music of the rigging—we needed no second invitation to " rouse and bit "—in another sense. We roused ourselves and bit eagerly at breakfast; indeed had we been fish we should most certainly have been caught for we disdained to nibbleand bit furiously. Once more aweigh and the peak up our destination : somewhere on the Welsh side we were told by one of the crew of a cockle-boat that "If we didn't" fatch " Mostyn we might" fetch "somewhere else." Embold- ened by this encouraging remark we stood out into the " Swash " and fought our way against a rather lumpy sea and wind, at first hot sufficient to control it. Thus little way was made. This however did not last long for the breeze freshened, coining in gusts from the Welsh hills, giving us an excuse for reeling. Reaching Mostyn Roads we took a fancy to run down towards Point of Air. With the breeze still freshening we ran into the mouth of Sluice [louse gutter, and up until she grounded. So when the tide had left us we made things snug—this remark applies to both the ship and her crew —and doft .shoes and socks the better to paddle about among the varying constituents of that composite shore. C'ose aboard we had soft mud mid-leg deep, then hard mussel covered gravel followed by beautifully clean sand. The sand for our virtues, the shelly gravel for penance and the mud for the cultivation of patience and resigna- tion in affliction. On the oozy bosom of this slough a Welshman had spread a small thread stop net.

On returning to the ship I found Tommy in eonfAb with this native. He had four nice flukes strung on a wire. "Now Tom," said I " are we two going to let this one take those lour ashore ?'' The Welshman intimated that he should arbitrable with a shovel he had with him. Fearing that the shovel might come to some damage

we comuroniised the matter for fourpence. Thus this late Welsh inv,asion, though ending in bloodshed, did so satisfactorily to both sides. And the spoils of that encount r met with quick dispatch and high apprecia- tion. And now where were we ? This Welsh sith of the Dee has a long fore-shore and dries out a good share of a mile at low water. Through ties long stretch of mud and sand the water from the hills finds its way to the river by sinu nis outlets, here in-euphemistically called "gutters." The one in which we find temporary lodgings, is "Sleuch-house gutter," then there is Llinyfar, Mostyn. and Llanerch-y-mor,and Greenfield, the last made by the everfiowing abundant waters of the flolywell. Our harbour is the one nearest the sea—some 5 or 6 miles from Rhyl—and is the navigable channel to tho Mostyn Col- liery Co.'s new pits, the workings of which extend far under the Dee. Two flats that followed us across, are here waiting at the mouth for the tide and the little tug to tow them up the narrow way which leadeth to car- bonaceous repletion. At the head of this funny little navigation we can see things are pretty closely packed— fiats and a large steamer and a barque which proved to be the "Jail" from Norway with coal-pit props. When the tide came we " shafted " our ship up with it, after waiting to get round the stem of a steamer that had per- versely grounded right across the channel. Making fast along side a moored flat, we started to go by tramp and train to Rhyl. The walk was an exceeding pleasant one. The healthy look of the vegetation alcne was a delight. The rich alluviums at the foot of the hills—rich by the denudation of these—is evidenced by the high luxuri- ence of the plant life, and the tall and shapely trees. Along the windings of this devious road—now on the flat—anon making a short excursion up the hills we found our way to Prestatyn station, from whence the small fee of 20. carried us into Rhyl.

After certain necessary performances—wholly unim- portant to the readers of this veracious narrative but helpful for its continuance—we strolled down to the beach to study the manners and customs of its habit sic. We found human nature to be very plentiful on and about that beach. Can't say that what we saw there gave one a very exalted idea of the intellectual outfit of its frequenters! The evidences one sees around us of a stilted conventional Grundyism and infl tted snobbery is not pleasant. Here where Mrs. Grundy comes, osten- sibly for change of air and relaxation, she still imposes ! upon her slaws the starch of a brainless conventionality. But mayhap the class who mostly hero resort find their relaxation and recreation in the assumption of a stricter conventionality than they are used to at home. The insane itch to appear grander than your neighbour, while incompatible with rational living, is the breath of life to the slaves of Grundy. For this they are willing cheerfully to sacrifice health, ease and their creditors. How comparatively deserted this parade—how lessened the paraders—did an unkind fate decree that au i bills should be paid ere the railway ticket be bought! But go they will, whoever pays for the show. The excursion must be executed,if an execution follows it. It is a relief to turn from the elders to the young sand architects , of the beach. Rhyl sands have little peace. When not I subject to the bulletings of Neptune's serried battalions or whirled around by Borean breezes these much vexed sands are subject to the invasion of a small army of active minors, ephemerally happy in building frail for- tresses to withstand the elemental onslaughts. Of course the beach would not be complete without its minstrels— whose Caucasian features belie their nigrhae pigment— for they, like the gentleman of like complexion, are not so black as they are painted, Here you can be weighed or caricatured photographically—you can pay your penuy—and it is wonderful what a number of oppor- tunities you hove of doing this—l say you can "down with your brown " to see things obscurely in camera, which you can see clearly outside, or, von may view the distant sea through the optic tube—having first downed the denarius.

Another way of " copping" the coppers is shown by the Boothites who are generally "on the job" where two or three (more or less) of thcse bits of filthy lucre can be gathered together. Here they exhibited the stock convert, who detailed his previcus bad habits in worse English and attributed his reformation to the work- ing of tho Lord within him. Whether this be so or no,the Lord only knows ! My opinion is that in such a case, if the man be taken out of himself by the infusion of any fervid enthusiasm the result will be much tke same. But, as it is impossible to infuse into an ignorant mind any cultured enthusiasm, the only alternative is a miraculous Salvationism, which is the chartered agency through which:the Architect of the universe is called down to do these small repairs. An old lady was affected even into tears by the harrowing " experiences" of the convert— though quite undisturbed by his jarring disruption of Our common tongue. If this man who details—and this woman who enjoys—religious lachrymosity—if of such is the kingdom of heaven—then I will take a back seat, if a lower one. Seriously, what good can come of such teaching—where erronious causes are attributed to the effects, where the imagination is allowol t ) over-run the judgment ? But onward. Here we have more con- vention—more artificiality —in shape of a pier and gaudy pavilion. The average Brown, Jones, and Robinson cannot do with nature " unimproved." For Mrs. Grundy, the seaside as nature made it, is not suffi- cient—it is, to her, uncivilised, so she and her votaries proceed to urbanize it in accordance with their own Vandalic taste. .
(To be continrel.)

div.head: PARMA MENI'ARY LEADERS.
div.p: PARMA MENI'ARY LEADERS.

What, asks a London correspondent of Cm Liverpool " Mercury," can Mr. Labouchere mean by saying that the man who has most increased his reputation in the present Parliament is Sir William Ilarcourt, and that he has now dispelled all doubts as to his ability to lead ? Except for his Budget, Sir William's grand achievement this session has been to be very much away from the House of Commons, and to hold his tongue when he was in it. Can Mr. Labouchere, by writing up a successor, have begun to write down his great chief ? f all the men in the present Parliament, those who have most distinguished themselves are Mr. Gladstone and Mr. , Chamberlain. Mr. Gladstone, within my recollection of his parliamentary career, has never shone to greater ad- vantage than he has done this year. His astonishing mastery in every detail of the Homo Rule Bill, the singular way in which, in his hands, the principles ot the measure are raised, whenever he speaks, into a higher plane of treatment than any of his opponents or col- leagues attain to, the completeness and swiftness of every faculty, and his super-abounding vitality, have demonstrated beyond doubt that he has no rival in the House, and gained for him the wonder and admiration of friends and foes alike. As a debating force also, Mr. Chamberlain has proved his power in a way he has never done before. Nothing could be better than his attacks upon the Bill. Were he not confronted by Mr. Glad. stone's great personality they would he truly formid- able, and it is the greatness of these attacks that brings out only more forcibly the supreme and transcending superiority of the Prime Minister, who stands in the breach alone and without an equal.

div.head: RAILWAY RATES.

ENORMOUS INCREASES ON COAL. Mr. W. S. Barrett, colliery proprietor, giving evidence on Tuesday, before the Select Committee relative to the operation of the revised railway rates, said that the in- creased cost of the carriage of slack and coal in South Lancashire and Cheshire would amount to £40,000 a year, that the additional cost of carriage in the South Wales coalfiAl would he £37,000 a year, and that the higher rates in South Yorkshire woui,l mean an extra cost in coal carriage of at least £lOO,OOO a year.

div.head: RUNCORN IMPROVERENT SIONERS. ELECTION Oh' CHAIRMAN.
div.p: RUNCORN IMPROVERENT SIONERS. ELECTION Oh' CHAIRMAN.

TIIE VACANCIES ON TIIE BOARD, A special meeting of the Runcorn Board Of Improvement Commissioners was lied at the Town Hall on Wednesday morning for the purpose of electing a chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. F. Wiswall presided, and there were also present Messrs. 11. J. Once, J. Fisher, P. Speal.man, R. Abel J. Dobson. J. Meadowcroft, S. Taylor, T. Lea, D. Bisbrown, W. Ilankinsnn, W. Humphreys, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E Marshall (secretaiy), and J. Barker (surveyor). -

div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. P. Speakman said that owing to the small atten- dance at the informal meeting of the meinhe rs the matter of choosing a chairman for the ensuing year hail been left over until the Board meeting that morning. Ile therefore moved that the Board form themselves into committee. This was carried imauimously and four ballots were taken before the reporters were called into the room again.—Mr. Speakman then said he had much pleasure in moving that Mr. Samuel Paylor be appointed chairman. He was sure that the B )ard would agree with him in saying that in appointing Mr. Taylor as their chairman they would be doing the town as well as themselves a good service. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Fisher seconded the motion and said he had not the least doubt that Mr. Taylor would fill the offim with honour and cre3it to himself and to the Board.—The motion was put to the meeting and carriA unanimously —Mr. Wiswall in leaving the chair said it was with 1, exceedingly great pleasure he vacated the chair ia I favour oh Mr. [viol', and he was glad that the Boar& had in the end been unanimous in their selection. In retiring from the chair lie could only express his extreme thanks to them for the way they had supported him: there ha t,een unpleasantocm and al Itn nimintt: had worked together hatmoalously. He greatly eliteemed the honour they conferred upon him twelve months ago and should always look back upon it with pleasure. There was he believed a great future before the town, and it would be known and noted all over the world, (Hear, bear.)—Mr. Taylor immediately after taking the chair proposed a vote of thanks to the retiring chair- man. Mr. Wiswall bad, he said, used every endeavour to conduct the business to the satisfaction of the Board. There had never been a chairman of that Board who had been more energetic thau Mr. Wiswall. (ll,!ar, hear.) —Mr. Speakman seconded the vote of thanks and said very good work had been done in the town through the influence of Mr. %Via wall and Mr. Meadowcroft.—Mr. Bishrown supported the vote and it was carried unani- mously.—Mr. Wis wall suitably responded.

div.head: Tll3 VACANCIES.
div.p: Tll3 VACANCIES.

The Board then proceeded to fill up two vacancies, one caused by the death of Mr. Coward and the other caused by the absence for six consecutive months Of Mr. Leach.—Mr. Speakman moved, and Mr. Fisher seconded. that Mr. John Wilson, architect and builder, be ap• pointed a member of the Mud in succession to Mr. Coward.—Mr. Ilisbrown moved, and Mr. L-2.a seconded, the appointment of Mr. William Handley.—Mr. Hankin- son moved that they should follow the course always :oiopted previously of electing the gentlnneu next on the poll at the last election. He move that Mr. Arthur tioup,rll beappointed.—Mr. Humphreys suggested that the Board go into committer to consider the question and that a ballot be taken.—This was done and Mr. Handley evidently received the highest number of votes, for when the reporters were again called into the room his appointment was carried unanimously on the motion of Mr. Bisbrown, seconded by Mr. Lea.—Mr. Lath whose long absence has been caused by a severe Illness was re-elected on the motion of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Hankinson.

div.head: TER WATER BILL,
div.p: TER WATER BILL,

The Lace Clerk announced that they had got their Water Bill through the Committee of the liaises of Par- liament the previous day with only two very slight alterations. They had obtained 60 years for the repay- tnent of the amount agreed upon and a term of 10 years for the payment of the costs. The Bill would be ready for the Royal assent very probably in the course ,ey fortnight. . This was all the public business.

div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE:
THE VACANCIES IN NORTH-EAST AND Sours.
EAST CORK.

The rits for the Parliamentary divisions of North- east and South-east Cork were received by tin Sheriff on Thursday. The former division was vacated by Mr. lluvitt in consequence of the bankruptcy procettaings • against him, and the latter by Mr. Morrogh, who re- cently retired. The nomination of candidates for both divisions will take place in Cork city on the 28th inst., and the. polling. should there be a contest in one or both divisi,dis, which is not thought probable, has been fixed for July Gth.

div.head: NUMEROUS PERSONS SERIOUSLY AFFECTED.
div.p: NUMEROUS PERSONS SERIOUSLY AFFECTED.

The whole of the fish in the Gwendraeth river, Kid. welly, near L'anelly, was, on Tuesday night, poisoned hv vitriol. Ifundieds of dead salmon and trout ,werti picked up on the banks on Wednesday and sold in the streets. On Thursday morning those who had eaten the poisoned fish were taken seriously ill, and considerable alarm rrevails. The medical men have numerous patients in hand, and grave fears are only entertained in two cases.

It will be seen from this that, though the Whole country has suffered, the more northerllyscountieshave had .more fertilis- ing showers than those ef the south. An. Essex farmer raises a pitiful wail over the' conditions Which prevail in his-county. The hay crop, we are informed, is not more than one-fifth of an average, and on a majority of farms .not more than half enough has been grown to. supply the horses with provender during the coming winter, to say nothing of the cattle and sheep. :In some dis- ;, tricts much of the-spring,eorn is not worth bar- Vesting and will be fed.off by sheep, while what is !eft will not be half an average crop. Fortunately, 111 these northern counties .agricultural prospects have not bc en so blighted as in Essex ; but even note the position of the farmer is not an enviable One just now.

At one time his victims, whose 'l.l.llll(lrings excited the commiseration and indigna- tion of the civilized world, were Groeirs, then Bill- latia"; now they are Armenians. Forty-six Trtnenian prisoners were lately put on trial before uriciall judges, forso-called political-olTences, and .o_ut Of these seventeen have been condemned to ;loath. Amongst the condemned are two:Protes- iatit ministers and professors at the American col- ega at Marsovan. As to the kind of evidence 11+1.13°n Which the Turks are prepared to condemn ose against whom a black mark has been placed, it ia said to ess°rs was at the charge against one of these pro - that he had in a sermon urged both ?adios to unite in Christian charity. At ! close of the war between Turkey and 'l_, Baia the latter country extorted from her. 472 f ersa a Prtdge of reforms in Armenia, but iloen,t the t"ards, attire instance of the Tory Govern- supremen in England, this article of the meaty was cancelled, and a bond was entered into 47ween Turkey and six _European countries for "a protection of the Armenians. None of the ti:lniaas then given by the Turkish Government t2B been carried out, and, as these trials show, and misrule are as rampant as ever. It 111.°113fnre behoves England, above all other mull-, trueal to see that the Armenians are not left tl tarlY without protection in the hands of their , bfttal and fanatical oppressors.

• A Fatally Maul; LARGE families are not popular Troubles, in France. According to census returns the births are barely sufficient to fill the vacancies caused in the popu- lation by death. This is a matter of serious con- cern to Prench statesmen and publicists. They 40 not wish to see their country fall behind other nations in the matter of population, and, above all/ they are desirous of keeping on something like equal terms with their prolific neighbours on the other side of OM Rhino. Amongst the ,reme- diets that have been proposed are the giving of Premiums upon families over a certain number,and the encouragement of matrimony by taxing bache- lors. But something more than this will be needed to poinflarize large families in France, if the account of the troubles of a family man published this week be correct. T 0 English people four children do not seem a very heavy endowment, yet it seems rto be a prohibitive number in the eyes of .reneh landlords. M. LACROIX is said to be a highly respectable man, but he finds it absolutely unpopsible to obtain a suitable habitation because el his four children. At ene place near Paris Where he applied for apartments he was received .14 a very civil way, until he mentioned that lie had rather a large family when the docr was had shut in his face. At another place he ad secured rooms and paid the usual preliminary Ihees,but when he turned up with his four children Was Politely 1t firm ly told that the "bargain .as off,' Not caring after this to endure any further rebuffs he has erected a large tent in the crest Of Vincennes and in this he and his family are rusticatino..

LOCAL NEWS.

RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. During the month of May 1.762 books were issued. RUNCORN SONS OF. TEMPERANCE. The fortnightly meeting of this association was liela on Saturday evening,under the presidency of Mr. Thomas J. Bolt. An interesting address was givm by Mr. Thos. Cooke. A conversation followed ,in which Messrs. Daniel Bisbrown, David Smith, John Junes, and Thomas Clarke joined.

DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORNIIN. On Wednesday afternoon, Mr. John Moores, general contractor, of 16, Sutherlan4-st., a welt-known Run- cornier'. idled at the age of 67 years. He was highly respected in the circle in which he moved. He leaves i Four cone to mourn his loss. The funeral takes place to- day in Runcorn Cemetery. When in want Of a CHASTE and ELEGANT WEDDING or BIRTHDAY PRESENT go to PRITCHARD'S, 51, High-at.—Ad. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES. The annual sermons were preached on Sunday by the Rev. W. H. Beeken, of Liverpool. In the afternoon the choir and scholars rendered the service of sone " Prim- rose Garth." The narrative vans read by Mr. T. &lowan Mr. A. Borthwick presided, On Monday evening a miscellaneous entertainment was given. SoSEPH PRITCHARD, 51, High-street, Runcorn, keeps SPECTACLES to soL all sights, from a shilling a air.—Ada. AN OLD OFFENDER SENr TO GAOL AT RUNCORN. On Wednesday at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. J. Brundiit and Mr. P. Speaktnan, a woman named Annie Ford. of Widnes, was sentenced to a months' hard labour for being drunk and damaging the cell by break- ing the windows. the woman had made frequent ap- pearances bef are the magistrates. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, Mgt- at., Runcorn.—Advt. ST. LURE'S CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The arrniversary of this school, which is doing a good work in the Canal-St. district, will be celebrated to- morrow (Sunday). The services will be held in Bethesda Congregational Church,and the preacher will be the Rev. J. D. Thomas, who laboured so successfully in Runcorn for many years. Full particulars in our advertisement columns; DEATH OF MR. TI3OIIAS SINGLETON, OF WIDNES. After a lingering illness. Mr. Juo. Thomas Singleton, butcher, Albert-road, died on Monday at the early age of 25 years. He was well kris.wn and respected in the town, and at the funeral on Thursday about 80 persons were present. The interment took place at St. Bodes Church, Appleton. Wreaths and crosses were contributed by many relatives and friends. Go to PRITCHARD", 51.1140 i-street. Ruucsrn, for the best Tire. GUINEA WATCH a workingman can have.—Advt. WIDNES AND THE ROYAL WEDDING. As will be seen from the list of subscriptions adver- tised in another column £llB 133. Bd. has been contri- buted towards •.ieletirating the royal wedding in July next by a treat to the day and Sunday school children. It is estimated that £3OO will be required and the Committee entrusted with the management of the affair met on Tuesdarnight, and came to the conclusion that it wou'd not be wise to make arrangements until half the sum requited was in hand. The Committee met again last night, ;to •make the necessary arrangements. ACCIDENTS AT WIDNES. On Saturday, a man named Edward Boyes was ad- mitted into the Accident Hospital, suffering from severe scalds ahceut the legs and left arm, sustained by falling into a vat of acid at Messrs. Mcliecknie's works on Saturday aaorning.—A bow named Henry Atherton, aged eight sra,tiving at 41, Mersev-road, was taken to the hospital in an exhausted condition on Saturday, through falling into the river whilst playing with a number of other children on the Promenade. He was attended by Dr. Donnelly. and was able to proceed home on Sun- day. If you want your WITCH REPAIRED by skilled workmen take it to PRITCHAItIiS.—Adrt ' SODDEN DEATH ON THE SHW CANAL AT RUNCORN. Oil Thursday, Mr. Worsley held an inquest at Run- corn Police Court on the body of Jno. Andrews, a Ship Canal labourer, aged 65 years, who had lodged in Fryer- st. The man fell down dead while at his work at the Big Field on Tuesday morning.—Dr. bleDougall said in his opinion death was due to the rupture of the large blood vessel leading from the left side of the heart. Witness had attended deceased for three months, and bad advised him not to work again, but three weeks ago lie did so without his (the doctor's) parmission.—The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical testimony. • ' PICNIC FROM RUNCORN TO AI:OEI2LE)/ EDGE. On Wednesday the Conlin ittee of the Assemble Hall and a number of friends had a picnic to Alderley -Edge. Starting at nine o'clock in a 'bus drawn by four horses, supplied by Mr. Connor of Warridgton, the party had a splendid 'drive of six hours through one of the most picturesque parts of Cheshire. A stoppage was made at a charming spot midway, where lunch was served in proper picnic style, and had there been a photographer, amateur ar otherwise there with his camera a picture would have been secured that would have been treasured as a souvenier of the Occasion. At five o'clock tea was partaken of at the Queens Hotel, and then a couple of hours were spent exploring the beauties of the village. The return journey was accomplished in quick time a change of horses being made ea route, and altog,eth er a most happy and enjoyable day was spent. ALLEGED THEFT OF A nORSHI AT WEsTON POINT. - On Thursday morning, at Ituncurn Police Court, he- fore Mr. Speakman, John Eloise was charged with I stealing a horse at Mato% Point, on the night of the 16th inst., the property of Mr. Leicester, boatowner, Stoke. The animal was placed in the &Able by Thos. Clutton, captain of the canal boat Ndson, they having : to wait for a cargo. It was subsequently missed, and information was given to the police. The horse Was I traced to Chester, where the prisoner tried to dispose of ; it for 104. thinking, however, that he was suspected, he bolted, Out vras apprehended at Stafford, where he was received into custody by P.C. Gregory. In reply to the charge he said " I am guilty.' —Superintendent Atherton applied for a remand for a week to enable him to complete the case, The prisoner had been guilty of a number of offences, one of which was horse tea ling as a bailre,for which he had undergone five years incarceration.Remantled for a week. „ DEIHODS ALLEGATIONS AGAINST WIDNES DOCTORS. On Thursday, at Widnes l'etty Sessions, before Messrs. flolbrook Gasifell, jun., and J. Stone, Alice Makin, 16, Bank-St., was sum:coned for not sending her child Jane regularly to sehool.—Mrs. Makin produced a doctor's certificate, stating that the child WAR unable to go to school for a month.—Mr. Dmby, clerk to the School Board said the Committee had no faith in those certifi- cates, as the parents could eat them at 3d. a head.—The magistrates' Clerk remarked that tint was a serious allegation to make.—The Clerk said lie could prove it, and he weuld call Dr. Hutchinson, oho had seen the child, to give his opinion as to the state of the child's lialth.—Dr. Hutchinson said lie accompaseied the Clerk to the defendant's house, and saw the girl in question. From her physical condition he could find nothing to prevent lie attending selinol.—After consultation the Bench decided to fine defendant 6d. and costs. - BOY DROWNED AT BOTTGAI LOCKS RESERVOIR. Mr. Wersler, the coroner. held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday morning, touching the deaths of James Gin; nine years of age, son of niter Gib. Insur- ance agent, 20, Waterlao-road, Runcorn, who was drowned in the bottom locks reservoir, opposite Leinster Gard, es, on Tuesday. Annie Gill, the mother, said shn sent her son an errand on Tuesday,and she did not again see him alive. She hat not known hiin play at this reser- voir. Richard Briscoe, a butcher, said he was near the reservoir about half-past seven, when he heard same boys shout that there was a boy in the put. He saw the boy sink. He had to run WOOS distance in order to get over the rails. The boy did not rise again. The grappling irons were fel elled from a but near by and the boy was recovered in about four minutes. He gave one "twitch." Dr. Brunten Was sent for, and every effort was made to restore animation but without avail. Witness could not swim. Had there been anyone pre- sent who could have dived, the boy might have been got from the water quicker.—Several jurymen observed that it was a very dangerous pool.—Mr. Bowyer said it V 4 as doubtful if anyone had gone DI whether he would have c.me odt alive again.—P.C. Neavin also gave evidence.—The Coroner said it was a very cal case indeed. It was a great pity that someone did not enter the water and try to fetch him out. If there had been aomoona there who had had the courage which most people in the diArict seemed to possess, the boy might now be alive and instead of holding, that inquest, might ve been m esenting a memorial to the Hum me Society. • —There was no evidence to show hew the boy got into the water, tort there Was no suspicion of foul play.—The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned," and the foreman (Mr. Shaw) said several jurymen had suggested that the railings should be made higher.

.• KILLED BY A CORPORATION HORSE AT WIDNES. On Wednesday afternoon Mr. F. A. Jones, the deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstances of the deitth of William Smith, aged 29, who had resided in Lacey-street. Mr. J. Cmik, assistant town clerk, was present for the Corporation. It apparel that deceased was a carter in the employ of the Corporation, and on Tuesday afternoon he was filling his cart at the night- soil dePet in Moor-lane when the horse took fright. Smith seized the bridle and was dragged about a hun- dred yards when he fell and the animal trampled upon him. He died in the Accident Ilospital a few hours later. It was staod that the horse was a spirited but not a vicious anima and had only ben recently pur- chased by the Corporation. A. verdict of accidental death was returned. The jury suggested that the Cor- poration should put two men in charge of newly bought horses until they had settle.d down to their wdrk.

HALTON WESLXTAN SUNOAT SCHOOL. The anniversary of this sc.hool was held last Sunday and Monday, the preachers being the Rev. A. P. Wat- son, of Preston, and the Rev. J. Hanby, of Runcorn. The extreme heat militated against the comfort of the worshippers ht thi services passed off very success- f oily. The total number cf scholars in the school is about equal to the entire number of scholars on the bo..ka ot the elementary day school in the Halton dis- trict, thus testifying to the extraordinary hold which , this has upon the population. Mr. Marshall, ileac to the Commissioners, and Mr. Alfred Norman, in their tour of inspection of all the schools in the Runcorn Wrsl,•yan S.S. Union. have reported that no school is in a st ate of 'greater efficiency. and only one other school I.Canide.n) is equal to it in the percentage of attendances. Tide remarkably successful state of -things is largely owing to the zeal and energy of a large voluntary staff of officers. More than ordinary, attention has been paid to the social department during the year and a pro- (trim-me of teas, entertainments, and lime.light lectures, kc., has been most highly appreciated. The coming Year is likely to be more than ever attractive as the Rev. S. Hanby is busy arranging a series of entertaining services for the long evenings which it is hoped will still increase the popularity of this institution. New scholars are received every Sunday and early membership in the flourishing sick and ciothing clubs is recommended. The ' working expenses last year were £26 and the result of this year's anniversary nearly £.29.

SANITARY INSPRCTORS IN CONFERENCE. On Saturday evening, the monthly meeting of the Sanitary Inspectors' Association (Liverpool Centre, North Western District) was held in the class-room of the Free Library, William-Brown-st., Liverpool, presided over by Mr. Ralph Norman, chief sanitary inspector for Warrington. Business connected with the council of the association hav- ing been disposed of, a general meeting was held, presided over by Mr. W. J. Stewart, stipendiary magistrate for Liverpool, when the annual presiden- tial address was delivered by Mr. H. Percy Boulnois. Mem. Inst. C.E. City Engineer, Liverpool.

Walter Warburton and Herbert Brooks, of Bank Quay, returning from Liverpool on Sunday in a yacht called the • Pink, had a curious adventure near Fiddlers Ferry. While rounding the bend they noticed two boys bathing near the bank and soon saw them both washed out of their dep.th by the tide. Warburton immediately put the boat about, and was just in time to rescue both lads, whose names were T. Eastman and W. Sharp. When pulled on board the l'ink both bathers were insen- sible, but after the application of restoratives they were able to proceed on their way home. Es. TO sn. WARRINGTON ITIGHWAY BoAnn. A meeting of the above named Highway Board was held in the Masonic Rooms Sankey-ston Wed- . nesday afternoon. The chair was taken by Captain T. B. Withington, J.P. There were also present Messrs. W. Gough, 11. Bate, 11. Armrod, J. Milling- ton, J. Rerfoot, J. Houghton, J. Grounds, J. Thomp- son, (Kirveyorl, and Mr. H. B. White (clerk).—The application from the Rural Sanitary Authority asking the Board to consent to their adoption of the Private Streets Act, 1892, was again considered. It was decided on the motion of Mr. J. Houghton, that the Board consent on condition that the streets be made with Newry setts instead of macadam.— Mr. Millington asked whether anything had been done in respect to the main road past Halton's Bridge at Panketh. The Surveyor thought the recommen- dations would be adopted by the County Council, and that the work would be proceeded with in a short time.—Mr.J.lloughton said for about five years the old footpath between Woolston and Thelwalt , had heed stopped by the Ship Canal Company, and people had been forced to go round to the pontoon bridge which was about 300 or 400 yards further round. When the footpath was taken over it yeas decided by the High way Board and Ship Canal Co. ' that another be substituted near the same place. Mr. Houghton thought the Canal Company intended to make the one the public had been forced to use for five years serve in lieu of one taken, which would be a great inconvenience. If the Highway ; Board had forced the Canal Co. to put a bridge over the canal at the tktne, it would have been better. t The Clerk was instructed to see if the Canal Corn- I pany had power to remove the footpath from where it was originally intended.

SINGULATt DEATH. John Brookes; a widower, aged 73, who lodged with Mrs. A. Longshaw, 4, Mill-st., died at the War- rington Infirmary on Monday from injuries lie received on the Wednesday previous. The deceased had obtained a livelihood as a horse farrier and had lodged with Mrs. Longshaw for about ten months. Ile had always enjoyed good health until the I'Wednesda3 previous to his death. Shortly after retiring to bed at about 10-30 on Wednesday night, he was heard to shout. Joseph Parker who lodges in the same house went upstairs and found the deceased lying on the floor. When asked what was the matter he replied "1 was undressing and my vest caught the knob or the.bed-post and threw my feet from under me." It was found that his thigh was broken, and Dr. Jack was sent for. The , doctor ordered Brooke's removal to the Infirmary. Ire was taken on the police ambulance and died at the Infirmary as above stated. An inquest was held at the Infirmary on Wednesday morning by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy-coroner.—Thomas Brookes was the first witness called, and he said deceased was his father. He saw him a week previous to the accident, and he was then in good health. He had lost his right arm and always wore a hook. He saw him after the accident: his right thigh was broken. Deceased said to him that he was undressing him- self when his feet slipped from under him. Cross- examined by the foreman of the jury he said the room floor was bare, and the room had just been washed.—Ann Jane Garnett, nurse at the Infir- mary, said deceased was admitted on Thursday morning suffering from a broken thigh). Ile died on Monday morning at 9-30 from the injuries sustained in falling. A verdict of "Accidental Death " was returned.

div.head: TRIPPING ON A TRICYCLE.
div.p: TRIPPING ON A TRICYCLE.
OUT WITH WARRINGTON CYCLISTS.
MY LURE BLUNT.

It was with a considerable amount of modesty, not to say misgivings, that I accepted the invita- tion of a Warrington cycling club to accompany them on a tour to Siddington. I cannot ride a bicycle; so I said if they would allow me, I would do the tour in a trap. But they said no—it would not look proper; and besides, they wanted me to experience the delicious enjoyment of travelling on wheels—a pleasure unimaginable to one who does not " ride.' Very good—l said, yours truly would trip along on a tricycle ; they were prefer- able for comfort to the bicycle. So I went to the hiring establishment and told the manager, as a special favour, to get me a good, reliable, strong tricycle—one that would be serviceable; not a! puny toy thing, that would all crackle up if you shaved a lorry wheel with it, or accidentally knocked a brick or two out of a wall. They had a !machine that would just suit me, he remarked, and he got the assistance of a boy and wheeled in something that looked like four trotting-buggy wheels. Perhaps I would like it painting a little, he asked. Never mind, I said, just scrape off the rust and make it a bit lighter, and squirm a little whitewash about the spokes to make it not, look too much like the bottom part of a hearse,and that would snit. The price he asked was threepence an hour, but no charge was to-be made for any damage done to the machine. This was kind ; I knew the machine could be bought for three and sixpence, but I kept low, and thanked him, just to give encouragement for the further collection of antiquities of that character.

Presently I got to Market Gate and commenced to pilot myself down Bridge-street. It was then that I began to shake hands with the joy of travelling on wheels. About every six yards, the machine would insist in tacking across the street.; this stopped the traffic. But I didn't care : I could plainly see people were turning green with envy to ride machine like that, and so I let in and made the old bone-shaker hum down that decline. Some- times I would run right past the head of a horse ; the driver would have to stop ; perhaps I would bear right down upon another vehicle ; the driver would have to stop. I blocked up the whole street in a jiffy—and you should have heard how those drivers ripped in and said things that preachers dare not utter in their pulpits. And how the People did laugh. They like to see a smart rider take the whip hand of a street full of traffic. By and by I got onto the straight road at Latchford and ploughed along with varying success, some- times not even running into passing carts. Bat I was not discouraged ; perhaps there might be a train handy at Latchford crossings, to run into ; for I meant to enjoy the privilege of damaging that machine without paying for it. Unfortunately, however, there was no train on hand at the cros- sings, so I passed and got on to Thelwall-road. I was getting considerably cramped up now, and felt as if I had been working a Corporation road roller. So the next time the machine ran into the hedge I had a rest. Before many moments had elapsed however, a tramp with an unkempt wealth of ginger coloured hair came along, with the breeze gently flapping his rags about. Ile shambled along listlessly, and finally sank don n on the grassy road side, right opposite. Ile threw a lazy glance across; then slowly shoved one foot through be- tween the "top " and sole of the boot, and fell to pairing his nails ; then lie did the other foot,just the same. Presently he got up with considerable effort, and walked slowly over to me. He said : " Excuse me, sir, lieve yew got a odd copper, sir." . .

I got my money out, and saw that I had an odd copper, so I said: " Yes, I have." "Thank yew koindly, eir." " Don't mention it—the information was cheap," I observed replacing the copper. He was a trifle staggered at first, but intimated that he wished to beg the money. This was a good opportunity for helping the man from his forlorn condition, so I waltzed into him with a mighty tall show of reproachful eloquence. I pointed out how useless and barren and tiispicable was the life of a mendicant who possessed strength to work and yet begged ; I drew a vivid picture of his insignific- ance in the world as compared with even the lowli- est beast that breathed ; I tried to stir up within him some flame of slumbering manhood, but he simply dumped himself down on the bank and expectorated tobacco juice. "It aint no blessed use—l aint a gewing to fly in the foice of Providence no more," he said. " The r good Book says we got to heve the poer with us I always. And it says yew've got to be content to walk in that path of bile in which yew are horned —howsomever humble. Don't it now ? ly Peter familier—yew know Latin ?—he and the old gal was both travellers; I been reared as one, and it flint roight to kick againat it. Providence knows what he's a-doing of—he ordains the poor; centuries ahead of their arrival. I believe in the B mit." Then he related a fact which had mede him more certain that his lot in life was that of a pauper. Once be found a bank-book and thinking it was the will of Providence that he should change his posi- tion in life, he tried to cash a cheque to buy some new clothes. But the shopman said "Wait a bit," and fetched a policeman, and the misguided tramp was sent to prison for three months, for aft lie pr - I tested he did not take the book from the owner's drawing-room table. He accepted the rebuke. There was some illusive philosophy in his argument so I did not retaliate but simply offered him reason- Ole terms to get out a tow line an I drag me cad

I gave him a piece of-rope and he set out on a ramshackling kind of a trot along he road ; by-and- by he dropped the trot to a walk, and finally he got. " mosying " along at the rate of about a mile an hour. When we got near Thelwall we olertook another traveller. They had a quiet confabulation together, at the end of which the tow line was transferred to the new man. I asked for an explan- ation and was informed that the contract bad beer sub-let. What was the price to the sab-cantre.etor inquired,and learned that it was three half Fence a mile,just half of what I had agreed to pay the tramp with the conscience. I told him he was a lazy schem- ing hulk, and paid hitn up sixpence, which I.e re- fused to accept at first, as he said we had travelled six miles. I shoved along to the station just in . time to catch a train for Altrinchain. So I entrained myself and the machine, for I meant to accomplish the journey somehow. I felt so pleased with tra- velling by rail that I booked from Altrineham to Knutsford. By the time I arrived here, the mem- bers of the club who had started out a few moments before me, were partaking of refreshments at the cyclist headquarters. I was congratulated all rouud upon the sharp trip I had made ; and I admitted it was pretty good time,af ter which everybody turned out and examined the machine, and then someone got held of a railway label which was on the :sidle, and which said: " L.& N.-W. Ry.—TIIELWALL, MT. lA. BLUNT. Per 3-0 train to Altrincham.

"Wrung ! Naw, there isna moach wrung! Oh, flaw !" I "Lost your youngest child, perhaps?" "Strange pup been killing the chickens?" "N -a-w "What, then r' "Why, oney this. I sat up for fourteen neights watching the finest gosling as ever was, grow. I watched it graw from the WiZ3 on a a,and spread and spread till it wur bigger'n a plumb. I watched by it as if it wur a sick choild—all the neight through, till I wur tired awt. Last Height I said to Polly oi thought we meight trust it till this morn- ing, and I went ter -bed and dreamed o' it awe night." "Yes."

"And when I woken up this morning it wur gone, and (bending closer) I con swear, by gosh I eon, that that lust prize un id the %le." Ile again lapsed into a meditative silence—a touching, pitiful, child-like grief, and he brushed ftom his manly cheek a tear ot disappointment. But later on he got a hit fresher, and vowed that next year he'd have his gooseberry photographed—then he'd detect them.

We stayed there for some time and made the in- habitants gloriously happy by giving them tunes on the piano, and singing sougs,and my friend with the artificial legs even paid for refreshtnants for them. As they got fresher they treated us more reverently ; they grew up from "Master" to then one of them in a kind of stibtnissive manner got to calling me "Squire," then they all did it. We left in time to catch the lust train home from Knutsford, and were escorted by four of the men who insisted upon" lighting" us along with lan- terns. WO could have been "me lards," if' he'd stayed longer, but even gratuitous presents of titular embellithments must be lust ; rather than the lot train

_ Then there was another similar label discovered which alluded to "a per 345 p.m. train to Kings- ford." It was a stupid oversight on my part to leave these things on, and it caused the most amicable of my friends to regard me with a chilly suspicion. I tried to dispel this feeling by narrat- ing the racing incidents which I had on the road with other better equipped cyclists. No matter how I exerted myself in this direction I couldn't raise a cheering look ; on the contrary, I hey seemed to shrink from me and look hurt—almost as though they suspected I was lying. We recommenced our journey and I was not left entirely behind this time. 1 kept up with a young fellow who had artiticisl legs and worked a tricycle with hand pedals. We had travelled perhaps eight miles by the time the shades of night had fallen—but Siddington didn't appear to be in the locality. Soon we were glad- dened by he sight of an illuminated hostelry, which we entered with an idea of getting our reckonings. But there was a surprise awaiting us. The huge room of the place was filled with ideal John Hodges —stout, burly farmer's men. They were seated along two long tables, and before each man there was spot of ceer and u dish of gooseberries. It had been the annual gooseberry show. Now ['wile who knows anything of Cheshire will be aware that in all millages almost, there la held a gooseberry show, which is regarded by the men as the greatest evenZ, of the year—except there he a funeral or a suicide or something more startling. A certain number of gooseberries grown by hims,a, are sub- mitted by each competitor, and the three finest berries take the first three prizes. The prizes had been awarded before we arrived and the men were well on in the midst of one of those conversations which prove that the country labourers have hearts

and intellects, though the latter often is shaded by) ship is restricted to men over eighteen years of iguorance. It was good to see the hearty jolley age." The protest concludes by urging the Bishop way that thOse great men devoted .themselves all to attend some typical P.S.A.. meetings,and expres- night long, to criticisms of geoseberries and other sing the belief that it would convert him from a matters ot a like character. But amongst them all deriding critic into a warm advocate and defender was conspicuous one man whc.se face bore a gloomy ot the P.S.A. Amongst the signatures attached to look, so deep and so intense that I twice wanted to the protest is that of the Rev. J. Yonge, leader of console him upon losing his wife and children. He the Warrington P.S.A. looked more down-hearted and despondent than a sick monkey. By-and-by I asked him what was wrong.

"Music in the Park" seems to be meeting with considerably more appreciation this year than in years gone by. The average amount collected as a rule used to fluctuate about the magnificent total of half-a-crown—with an occasional foreign coin.. Last Sunday but one however,no less than .£2 4s. sd. was collected, whilst last Sunday .£1 78. 2d. was received.

By the way this (Saturday) afternoon,Mr. Down's excellent band have arranged to discourse a well- selected programme in the park, and the Mayor and Mayoress, and members of the Town Ceuncil will be in attendance, and, another thing which is quite acceptable, it is the intended to place as many chairs as possible in the ring to supply the serious lack of sitting accommodation which has been so- much complained of lately. All I hope is that this extra accommodation will always be procurable and not end with this special visit of civic dignitaries. In case the weather is inclement,the band will give their performance in the Drill Hall,the use of which has bedn kindly granted by Colonel Greenall and the officers of the Volunteer Corps.

A question which has cropped up spasmodically at the Town Council meetings for a few years past, is the advisability of providing of mqre recreation ground. None of the council—except one or may be two—seem to have seen the necessity for such a provision. Now I can suggest a very simple method by which they will learn conclusively that a recreation ground is required. Let those undecided members go down into Museum-street any evening during the week. They will there see playing on the open ground, and even on the road no leas than a dozen cricket teams—and if they can walk down the street without getting struck with the impres- sion I hare named and several cricket balls, then I very much mistake their powers of perception, and want of physical alacrity.
MERLIN.

div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

It is' quite clear from the proceedings at the an- nual meeting on Wednesday that Runcorn Com- missioners have broken through the unwritten rule that each member should occupy the chair in rotation, and it will be generally agreed that they have done wisely. There was great divergency of opinion as to who should occupy the position for the ensuing year. Differences, however, were set- tled in Committee by four ballots, and then Mr. Samuel Taylor was appointed unanimously. Mr. Taylor occupied the position a few years ago and it is a great compliment to him that he should have so soon had the honour again conferred upon him. The choice could not have fallen upon a more popular and estimable gentleman.

Mr. Wiswall, who was cordially thanked for hie services, has held the reins during a most event- ful year. It will ever be remembered that the \Waterworks were acquired during his chairman- ship. Ile took a most active part in the matter, his experience as an engineer being invaluable and it is to be hoped that the undertaking will be successful and profitable_ It is regrettable that we have not had the Technical Institute under weigh during the year. The attempt to raise money by subscription has almost totally failed. only the Vicar, (Rev. Canon Maitland Wood) and Mr. P. Speakman having contributed, and it is quite clear that the Commissioners will have to carry out the work with the rates at their command. Mr. Taylor will confer a great benefit upon succeeding generations if be can succeed in launching this pro- ject during his year of office.

Towards the £3OO required to give the children a treat in commemoration of the Royal marriage, only £7O had been contributed up to Tuesday night, and the commltte3 were unable to proceed with their arrangements. •

div.head: HEALTH OF WARRINGTON. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. J. 11. Gornall, medical officer of health, has just issued his annual report upon the health and mortality of the Borough, together with an account of the sanitary work acc(implished during the year ending 31 December, 1892. The report states that the estimated

POPULATION AT MIDSUMMER in 1892 was 54,084, whilst the area of the town was 2,004 acres, the density of the population being 26 per acrea. There were then 10.394 inhabited houses against 10.190 the previous year. The total number of births , was 2,161 of which there were 1.111 males and 1,050 females, making a birth rate oi 39-9. The total num- ber of deaths was 1,267, 665 males and 602 females making a death rate of 227. This includes 44 that took place at Aiken-street Fever Hospital, and 40 at the Hope Hospital (smallpox). The most densely populated por- tion of the Borough is reported to be the insanitary area in St. John's Ward ; there the population is about 300 persons per acre. The estimated population in 1851 was 22,894, and the rateable value was £47,849 for Warrington township, and £4,060 for the Latchford township. The present rateable value' of the town is £156,078 Warrington township, and £13,363 Latchford township. This shows a decrease of £lOO in the Latch- ford township and an increase of about £l,OOO in War- rington township. INFANTILE MORTALITY. Of the 608 deaths registered last year in children under five years of age,34l were infants under 1 year. It was 3.2 higher than the rate during the year in the larger towns of ngland, and 4.1 more than that for the rural dis- tricts and smaller towns. In 1891 the number was 350 out of 595, 1899 351 out of 583, 1889 318 out of 570. Cal- culated by the proportion of deaths under 1 year of age to the births registmed,the infant mortality in Warring- ton for the year 1892 was equal to 157 per 1,000 against 155 in 1891, 171 in 1890, and 156 the average of the 5 years (1886-1890) INFECTIOUS DISEASES. The adjoining areas of Runcorn and Warrington Rural have now adopted the Act iui" the Notification of Infec- tious Diseases,but are still without any prOPi5101:1 for the laOlatien and treatment of Zymotic Diseases ; and as the portions of their said Districts adjoining the Borough aro the most populous, and have direct communication with vent town by business and schools, it is imperative that at a very early date some united action should be taken to secure hospitals to deal with smallpox, the latter now in our midst, and cholera looming in the distance. BMALL-PDX. Alluding to the small-pox epidemic Dr. Gornall stated that as the assistant medical officer had prepared a report upon the subject he would refrain from going into the matter in detail. He stated that since the in- troduction of the disease in July there had been 489 cases notified or discovered up to December 31st. Out of that number there were 55 deaths or a little over 11 per cent, of the number notified. This is equal to I'ol per 1,000 of the population. 'rho distribution of deaths from this disease in the several wards of the town was as follows :—Town Hall, 6; Whitecross, 9; Bewsey, 6; St. Sohn's, B; Fairliekl, 1; •Orford, 14; Howley, 5 St. Amalfi, 1; Latchford, 5. St. AMUR'S ward has, the lowest general death-rate. of any ward in the town, only nine being recorded. The largest death-rate was ReWsey, the number being 41, of which 23 were caused by scarlet fever. In making further reference to the epidemic the doctor says :—"The year has been one of great anxiety to your staff, and evils that I have fre- quently foreshadowed have actually occurred, giving rise to the dissemination of disease among the patients other than for which they were admitted. Cases of small-pox developed among the patients admitted suffer- ing from scarlet fever in August and September, due to cases of small-pox which we were obliged to take in in those months, as well as to cases of small-pox being sent in as scarlet fever. I regret to say that one unvac- cinated child that had recovered from scarlet fever died thoin small-pox, and another (again unvaccinated) who developed the disease soon after being discharged well from scarlet fever, died at the Hope Hospital."

div.head: SCARLRT FEVER.
div.p: SCARLRT FEVER.

"To add to our difficulties in the past year" adds the doctor " this Infectious disease was widely preva- lent. The total number of cases notified was KO, of these 66 were fatal—equal to 13 per Gen-. t fO. the eases, and 1.2 per 1,000 of the population. Of this number 394 were removed to the Fever Hospital, 37 provinz fatal, or 9 per cent. • of the remainder 115 were treated at home, 29 died, or '25 per cent."

div.head: INFLUENZA.
div.p: INFLUENZA.

_ This disease, associated with hing affections, having nearly disappeared at the end of 1891, made its appear- ance again in Jannary, and continued to mark its pres- ence by additions to our deaths until the end of June. The number of deaths from influenza from January 9th, 1892, to 14th May, was 23, whilst from lung disease the number was 148. INSANITARY PROPERTY.

Statistics are submitted respecting the insanitary con- dition of the area condemned lone ago by Dr. Gornall— namely, the area known as the Dial-st. and Cockhedge area, consisting of two acres of courts, or cal de ears. in which dwell 623 people. Concluding, the Medical Officer reports :—" During the year I have certified the following houses as unfit for habitation : Twenty,eight houses in Erwood-at., Nos. 2 to 28, and 1 to 27, still occupied and no alteration. Foarteen houses in Pier- point-st., Nos. 94 to 120, still occupied and nu alteration. Nine houses in Turner-st.and Pinshpplard,still occupied land no alteration."

HOUSEBREAKING. • _ Housebreaking and burglary seem to continue at S. Helens, for on Minday night, it is said, the lock-up shop of Messrs. P. and W. Harrison, chemist and druggist. Boundary-road, was broken into, and about £2 worth of patent medicines and other articles stolen.

There appears to be a great amount of interest taken in the water question at Penketh. The iVes- leyan schoolroom was crowded at the public meet- ing on Thursday night, and so voluble was a large portion of the meeting that the, Chairman had con- siderable difficulty in stemming the current 'of talk. Mr. Parker who opened the question gave tho case from the manulacturer's, and also in reality from the workmen's point of view, as in this case, if the works suffer from want of water, the men as well as the masters suffer in consequence. There was a considerable amount of opposition to the proposal to have a fresh water supply, chiefly coming from property owners. div.head: SAD RESULTS OF THE HEAT AT WAR-
div.p: SAD RESULTS OF THE HEAT AT WAR-
ItINGTON.

-- Several cases of sunstroke have been reported from various parts of the neighbourhood. On Sunday attlr- noon a man named William Davies, who is employed in the Permanent Way Department, of the London and North-Western Railway Company, sras engaged at Moore, near Warrington, and, owing to the excessive heat, he became so alarmingly ill that Ms mates removed him to Crewe as speedily as possib'e. He was taken to the Company's hospital, and his case is so serious that the doctors only entertain faint hopes of his recovery. Mr. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest at the Walton Arms, on Saturday, touching the death of Robert Hol- land, 63 years of age, a land agent residing at Frodsham. wka died suddenly on the previous day. It appears that he called to see Mr. Thomas Ball, a farmer at Acton Grange, and left about 11-30, saying that he woulct have a look at the new bridge over the Ship Canal and then go borne by train. Some time afterwards, Henry Thelwell, a signalman on the Ship Canal, saw deceased. going in the direction of the bridge, and then saw him on his way back. Deceased did not pass the signal-box,. an the sis,mahnan on looking out again, saw him lying against the hedge bank, and on going up to him found that he was dead. Dr. Barton. of Frodsham, said he was of opinion that the deceased died from heart disease accelerated by the heat.—A verdict to this effect was returned.

div.head: PROPOSED SWIMMING CLUB FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: PROPOSED SWIMMING CLUB FOR WARRINGTON.

Now that Warrington has a bath worthy of the name, it has been thought desirable that a swim- ming club should be formed in the town. In order to see what arrangements could be made in this direction, e public meeting was called at the Coun- cil Chamber of the Town Hall, on Wednesday night.. The attendance, however, was not 'very large. On the motion of Mr. Diggle, Mr. S. Kenyon was elected. chairman.—The CHAIFOCIN after stating the objects of the meeting, said that they all knew how healthy and enjoyable an exercise swimming was. It might also be exceedingly useful in saving one's own life or other peo- ple's lives. He also thought it was beneficial to the mind as well as the body. Ile hoped that those present would give their views on the subject freely.—The Rev. H. V. nom said that he had had no sxperionce of swimming clubs, although he had been a swimmer almost as long as he could remember. He would move that it was desir- able that a swimming club bc formed,so that they could make good use of the new bath which they were proud to consider was one of the finest in the Kingdom. (Ap- plause.) lie thought a swimming club should be largely educational to make swimming a subject of instruction. Of course, he supposed there would be something done to encourage higher branches of fancy swimming, but , , he hoped they would not confine themselves to that.—. • Mr. J. SUTTON seconded the motion. He said they had at-one time a swimming club in Warrington. He wished that they could have their rules and regulations so that they could form their plans in that guide.—The motion Ott being put to the meeting was carried unanimsusly. It was decided to refer the question of entrance fees,etc., to a committee, and on the invitations being given to those present to give in their names as possible members, o good number availed themselves of the opportunity.

div.head: QUEEN'S MEMORY.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S MEMORY.

An intere:ting story of the Queen's retentive memory is told by Mr. Stead in his character sketch of Lady Henry Somerset in the " Review of Reviews." In her cal ly days Lady Henry Somerset was very punctilious al)!Int her rank. On one occasion she was taken as a child te see the Queen. Her Majesty called her " little Isabel." Wnereupon the offended little aristocrat, tos- sing her head, said with aggrieved emphasis to her amused Majesty, "Lady Isabel." A dozen years passed, and the young girl, now a woman grown,was presented at Court. As the debutante bent forward to kiss her hand, the Queen's marvellous memory asserted itself. The old scene flashed before her mind, and her Majesty said, with a pleasant smile and an unmistakable " Lady Idabel."

div.head: JOHN BRIGHT'S LIBRARY.
div.p: JOHN BRIGHT'S LIBRARY.

Talking of John Bright and his books, Mr. J. T. Mills, his mast recent biographer, says :—AI years passed on one room became too small to contain the rapidly-in- creasing collection of books, many of which acr 11 e pre- F.. ed to Mr. Bright by their publishers or authors, and the volumes over-flowed into the dining-room and break- fa st room, the latter of which was itself a library in all but the name. Large as was his acquaintance with rooks, it WAS equalled by his love of them. what," he once asked, "is a great love of books? It is som4hing like a personal introduction to the ereat and good men of all past times. Books, it is true, are silent as you see them on their shelves ; Gut, silent as they are, when I enter a library I feel as if alinoA the dead were present, and I know if I put ques- tions to these hooks they will answer me with all the faithfulness and fulness which have been left in them fly the great men who have left the beats with us. . . I am bound to say—and if any one cares Very mudi for any-thing else they will not blame me—l say to them, you may Intro in a house costly pictures and costly ornaments, and a great variety of decoration, yet, Co far as my judgment goes, I would prefer to have one comfortable room well stocked with books to all you can give me in the way of decoration which the highest art can supply."

div.head: PONTOON DOCK FOR THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: A PONTOON DOCK FOR THE SHIP CANAL.

The "Newcastle Chronicle" nye :—The Edwards Shipbuilding Company, Limited, Howdon, are at present constructiug a large iron pontoon dock for the Man- chester Ship Canal Pontoons and Dry Docks Company, Limirro.. The dimensions are 300 ft. long by 701 t. broad, and 31f5. to the top of the towers, There are forty water-tight tanks, each seven feet deep. ahich will be by four inlet valves, each 181 n. in diametex, two on el • her side. These valves will be worked from the top of the towcr:k. For the purpose of pumping out the wa,cr after tne dock has been sunk and the vess,l to be ' docked lIRR been placed on the blocks, large centrifu:Sl pumps by Meisrs.Tangye, of Birmingham, will be fitted.: lie whdle of the machinery will be placed at the fore. part of the dock, and will include, in addition to the pumps, two boilers, nine feet diameter and nine feet long, by Messrs. J. T. Eltringham and Co., South Shields. The. dock is Mr. Alexander Taylor's patent, and similar to that built by Messrs. Swan and Hunter, of Wallsend, f w the st alls'end Pontoon and Dry Docks Company, Limited. Tho worlc was commenced in February last, and has been so expeditiously carried out that it is hoped to launch the dock towards the c-nd of next month. It will then be towed round the csast an delivered at Ellesmere Port, about six miles up the Manchester Ship Canal. The work has been carried out under the inspec- tion end supervieion of Mr. Sharer, general manager, and Mr. A. Swan, otitsule manager, of the builders' firm, and Mr. A. Taylor, the patentee, and Mr. Harrold on behalf of the owners. There have been used in the construction nt the dock about 1,500 tons of iron and nearly 400,003 rivets,
