div.head: MAGISTRATES.
div.p: THE MAGISTRATES.
RESULT OF SSLLING ONE'S OWN COFFEE.

Thomas Sutcliffe, Sankey Bridges, was brought before the Warrington county magistratcs on the charge of selling Alb. of coffee containing 35 per cent, of chicory. P.C. Duncan proved the case. Mrs. Sutcliffe who appeared for her husband said that although she had a Shop, she scarcely sold any coffee. The coffee com- plained of was some for the consumption by her family. She only bought a lb. at once, and always had it mixed with chicory. She rarely sold more than an ounce at once. The Bench fined defendant ss. including costs.

div.head: BREACH OF THE FACTORY ACT.
div.p: BREACH OF THE FACTORY ACT.

At the Warrington .133 rough Court yesterday before ,i'derman Harrison (chairman), Alderman Wright, Dr. °email, and Councillor Roberts, Messrs. Parkinson and Co. Manor Tannery, Latchford, were charged with corn rnitting a breach of the Factory Act by not keeping a register of a young person employed by .the company, . . .

, . and also wit( failing to procure a certificate within seven days of the same young person, Mr. C. W. Shaw, Her Majesty's Inspector of Factories, said that he visited the place on May 10th, and found a boy named Thomas Wheeler in the defendants' employ. The firm had no register. A clerk who appeared for the firm said that they were ignorant of the law. The chairman, however, said that ignorance of the law was no excuse, and fined defendants ss. and costs in each case. Alt INCORRIGIBLE BOY. _ . .

. At the Warrington Borough Court on Thursday,before Alderman Sutton and Coancillor Fleming, Austin Ridg- way, a boy thirtees years of age, was charged with stealing a pair of child's boots, valued Is. 9d., the pro- perty of Freeman and Hardy's Boot Company, on June 15. Prisoner had been employed by the Boot Co., up to Thursday last week, and then left. On Wednesday the father found a pair of boots in the boys" pocket, and he at once took them to the manager of the boot shop who identified them as belonging to the company. The man- ager did not wish to press the case, hat the boy's father gave information to the police, and Detective Monaghan , arrested the bey on Wednesday night. Prisoner's father said that he was incorrigible and he could do nothing with him as he was always stealing things its the house. Be would like him to be sent to a house of correction. The magistrates ordered prisoner to be sent to St. Anne's Industrial School in Liverpool for three years. PUBLICANS FINED.

At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednesday, John Jackson, of the Fiddlers Ferry Inn, Penketh, was charged with selling some whiskey containing 30 per cent, of water to John Fligginbottom on the 26 h Mr. Jenkins who appeared for the defence, admitted that the whiskey supplied was as stated by the police, and that the analysis was right. He pleaded that the hot weather of the past weeks had caused a great amount of evaporation in the spirits, and this accounted for thel percentage of water found in it. His client had not the slightest idea that there was such a large percentage Of water. Defendant was sworn and supported his solici- tees statement. The Bench' indicted a penalty of 20s. and costs. Jon Warburton of the Chapel House Inn, was also charged with serving some gin which con- tained 33 per cent, of water on the 20th ult. DIP same defence was raised as in the last case,and the magistrates fined defendant 103. and Costs. DISGRACEFUL CONDUCT OF A DRUNKEN MAN.

Before the Warrington magistrates, on Monday, John Molarney was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Stanley-st., on Saturday night, and also with assault- " a boy named Peter John Cummings at the same time and place. P.S. Taylor had received complaints on Saturday night of prisoner's disorderly conduct,and that he had kicked an old man and the complainant. He Went in search Of him, and at length found him creating a disturbance in Stanley-Bt. He at once locked him up. Peter John Cummings, who was called, stated that he was walking along Sankey-st. and as be passed prisoner, who was very drunk, prisoner deliberately kicked him on the shoulder. Another witness was called to corroborate the boy's statement, and who also saw an old man badly kicked by prisoner. Prisoner expressed his contrition as he was drunk at the time. Mr. Wm. Pierpoint, one of the magistrates, was of opinion that the publicans who served the drink to these men ought to he summoned. Prisoner as fined 20s. or a month's hard labour in de- fault.

div.head: BENIGHTED COUNTRYMAN.
div.p: A BENIGHTED COUNTRYMAN.

Henry Beard was brought before the Warrington magistrates, on Monday, on the charge of being on the enclosed premises of Wm. Molyneux, Battershy-lane, at 6 30 a.m., on Sunday, with intent to commit a felony. P.C. Clough stated that Molyneux kept a large number of fowls, and was frequently missing some of them. On Sunday morning witness was called into Mr.Molyneux's yard, and there found prisoner lying asleep on seine hay in an outhouse. Re had forced the door open and broken the hinges. The fowls were running about the yard and it was this circumstance that called Mr. Molyneux's attention to the presence of the prisoner. Witness took him to the Police Station. Mr. Molyneux corroborated the officer's statement, and Inspector Spinks said that he had seen prisoner in the "Sixpenny" at about 3 p.m. on the same morning. Prisoner denied any intention to steal anything, but said that he worked at Padgate, and coming into the town on Saturday night, he took too much beer, and it was too late to go home, and he went into the place where he was found, to have a sleep.— Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprison- ment.

div.head: BATCYo STONETIIRO'WERS.
div.p: A BATCYo STONETIIRO'WERS.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, Edwd. Buckley (17), 6, Derby-st., Wm. Whittaker (16), 13, Manchester-road. Wm. Brad hlw (17). 10, Eldon-at., Ernest Burton (18),60,Schoe1-brow, David Wi!cocks (18), 8, Manchester-road,Thomas Austin, jun.(16),112, School. brow, Charles Taylor (18), 113, School-brow, James Stockton (16), 54, Forshaw-st., and Thomas Travis (17), 3, Refuge-square, were each charged with throwing stones to the danger of passengers in Orford-avenue, on the 11th inst. P.C.'s Turner and Hampson were on duty in plain clothes on Sunday, and saw all the defendants throwing at a gate, they afterwards threw at the railway bridge in the Avenue and also at a lamp post. The two officers then got their names and reported them. The Chief Constable said that he had received a large number of complaints about stone throwing in Orford, and Mrs. Beamont was afraid to come out of her house on Sundays owing to this nuisance. He would not press the case that morning, as the defendants bore previous good characters.—Defendants were each fined is. _ A REGULAR RICT _

Wm Burke, Samuel Pownall and Hannah Makin, all of Gee-st., were charged at the Warrington Borrugh Court, yesterday, with fighting in Gee-street on the 17th inst. Wm. Burke and Mary Burke were also charged with assaulting Hannah Makin on the same date. P.C. Evans Said that on Saturday from information received I 0 proceeded to Gee-street, and there found Wm. Burke suffering from severe wounds in the head. Hannah Makin had also a bandage over her head. When brought together, they at ince consraenced to accuse each other of assault. Witness reported them all at the police Station. William Farder stated that Wm. Burke was struck by Pownall with a poker, and was also struck by Mrs. Makin.—Mary Ann Burke on the other hand said that Wm. Burke gave Mrs. Makin a violent blow on the bead with a stick, and that Burke was not ass tutted at all. A number of other witnesses were also called who contradicted each other in -every particular. The mag- istrates finally dismissed the charge against Mrs. Mikin, and bound Samuel Pownall, and William Burke over to keep the peace fr six months, in a surety of £lO. Burke was also fined 10s. and costs for the assault on Mrs. Makin.

div.head: BEFORE
div.p: BEFORE
CRIIELTT TO HORSES.

Edward Carlisle and Fred. Carlisle were each charged at the Warrington Borough Court yesterday, with allow- ing a horse to be worked while in an unfit state, on the 14th inst. Inspector Dowty, R.5.?.0 A., said that he saw Frederick driving a horse in Golborne-street on the above date. It appeared to be very lame, and he found that it was suffering from pain in the off-leg. He told defendant to take it home which he did. The horse belonged to Edward. P.C. Turner corroborated,and the magistrates fined Edward 103. and costs and Frederick Si. and costs.—Maurice Mulchar, 4, Dalman'alane was alas charged with beating a horse on the 14th inst. Inspector Dowty said that he saw prisoner coming up 13uttermarket-street on the above date. Ile was flogging the animal severely with a whip. The whip was an ordinary driver's whip, but at the end a number of gutter percha lashes were plaited. The flogging caused a r umber of marks to rise on the skin. P.C. Bell stated that the defendant flogged the horse from Butter= rket- street toCorporation-street. Defendant was fined 103. land costs or 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: MINOR CASE.S.
div.p: MINOR CASE.S.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.—Before Councillor EL Roberta (in the chair),
and Mr. R. Garnat.

?Join DESERTERS.—David Dean was charged with be- g's deserter from the Royal Artillery stationed a Templemore. He applied to Lance Corporal G. Wayne on the 15th inst. for enlistment in the Militia, when he found out that he seas a devrter. William Lovett Was also charged with being a deserter from the Yorkshire Light Infantry stationed at Belfast. He was caught by Lance Corporal William Coupe. •Both prisoners were committed to Strangeways to await an escert. The usual reward was granted to both officers.
INDECENT CONDUCT—Michael rforan, employed at the Whitecross W rks was sent to gaol for one month hard labour for indecently exposing himself in Chorley-street, on several occasions.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (chairman), Alderman Holmes and Harrison, Messrs. W. Pierpoint and S. Wright. FALSE ArrEsmurroN.—For making a false attestation at thetime of enlistment in the army, George Hall was I fined 403. including costs or 14 day's imprisonment, and Sergeant Stacey received the customary reward. MARKET THlEF.—Sarah Ann Hoyles, 4, Buckley's 'Court, off Haydock.street, was charged with stealing a pair of boots valued 2s. 61., the property of Joseph Frisby, and also a pair of stockings and woman's corset valued 33. 91., the property of James Weston in the Market Place on Saturday night. Prisoner had bought a pair of boots from Mr. Bowers, the manager of Frisby's shop, when Mrs. Bowers observed her pick something up from the stall, and prisoner was seen to pick up a corset off Mr. Weston's stall which was in charge of Eliza Ellison. Mr. Bowers then C 3 me up and found that she had two pairs of boots and stockings in her position. Meanwhile Eliza Ellis2n had informed P.C. Barlow, and that officer took prisoner into custody. This being prisonars second offence, she was sent to gaol for one month. .

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this cffenee Thomas Barrow arid Joseph Peel were fined 53. and costs or seven days ; James Lee was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. For being drunk in the Swan entr3 off Bridge-street on Saturday night. John McDonald was fined 23 6d. Joseph Langon was fined 23. 61. for being drunk in Clothall Yard on Sunday morning. _ .

ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.—John Morris was charged with being drunk and disorderly and 'so with assault- ing P.C.'s Hardy and Monks on Sunday morning. Prisoner was lying on the ground of the Ship Yard on Sunday morning, in a very drunken condition when the officers attempted to remove him, he gave them some very severe kicks, and they had great difficulty in.cet- ting him to the police station. Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs or a montl.'s hard Ist our. _ _

- INDECENT HEHAVIOUR.—Jonatlian Birchen was charged with acting indecently in Longford-street on Sunday afternoon. The evidence was very weak, and prisoner was given the benefit of the dcubt and dismissed. HAVING DOGS WITROUT LICENSE.—WiIIiam Berry, 11, Stephen-streer, was summoned for having two dogs nti the 11th inst. without having a license, and was fined Bs. in each case. _ . _

A DANGEROUS PLAYTHING.—John William Bradb-ry (16). 171 Winwick-road, was charged with discharging stones for a catapult on the 11th inst. P.C.'s Turner and Hampson each deposed to seeing the defendant use the catapult in Winwick-road and the magistrates in- flicted a penalty of 2i. Ott. and costs.

TUESDAY.—Beforo Mr. It. Garnett (in the chair) and Dr. Starkey Smith. TUE HOTTEST TEMPERED WOMAN IN WARRINGTON.— ' Margiret Lowe, Foundry-st., was charge_d with being drunk and disorderly and also with assaulting P.C. HAVING HIS REVENGE OUT OF TIRE WINDOW —William Welsh was charged with breaking a window in Burton- wood on thd 11th inat., doing damage to the amount of ss. Patrick Conway, the complainant, said that at about eleven o'clock at night on the above-mentioned date, defendant came to see his sister who lived next door. The gate was fastened by a chain, and he alm,st shook the gate post down before witness could open it for him. Defendant then went and rattled at his sister's door, but no one came to open it for him. Wit- xess told him to go home,-but he took out a knife and I smashed witness's window. Witness afterwards pushed him out of the yard. Defendant said that he did not smash the window until he had been struck by corn-

plalnant. Defendant was ordered to pay the damages and also the costs of the sumtnonse3. THE ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.

The Royal Agricultural Society of England opened its annual show at Chester,on S tturday. On Monday a fire broke out at one of the implement stands in the show yard, but fortunately was prevented from spreading. The Mayor and Corporation gave an official receptioe to the Prince of Wales at half-past six. In replying to an addressor welcome his Royal Highness thanked the Cor- poration for their cordial words, in which they referred to the approaching marriage of the Duke of York. He lamented that the present position of agricultural affairs was so discouraging, and that there were no signs of im- provement. The emulation which such shows engen- dered and the educational benefits derived from practical and scientific knowledge could not fail to contribute in giving confidence and assistanee to all those who were striving to overcome the present difficulties. The Roy-al Agricultural Show was continued at Chester on Tuesday, under favourable auspices, the attendance being 20,959. At the annual meeting of governors of the Royal Agricultural Society, under the presidency of the Duke of,Westminster, the Prince of Wales moved a vote of thatlll9 to the Mayor and Corporation of Chester, for the cordial reception the society had received. The Duke of Devonshire was elected President for the ensuing year, and it was decided to hold the next show_at Cam- bridge. . . _

Owing to the great inrush of people to Chester, on Wednesday,the resources id the railway companies were again taxed to the utmost. Notwithstanding the gigantic preparations to cope with the traffic to the show and river carnival, they were unable to fully meet the demand, and at two o'clock in the morning hundreds of people found themselves on the station platform of the London and North-West-rn and Great Western Railway companies, having failed to find accommodation in the numerous heavily-laden trains which had been des- patched. No beds were obtainable in the city, and the unfortunate passenirers had to wait in the railway station all night for the early morniag trains.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR.
div.p: A MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR.
A GHASTLY KEEPSAKE.

PARIS, THllRSDAT.—Telegrams from Pau report that a most mysterious affair is being investigated by the police. It appears that three years ago a priest named Laporte came to Pau, where he lived in the greatest retirement. Shortly before his death last month he asked that a small box under his bed should be buried with him. His request was, however, not complied with, and the box on being opened was found to be richly lined and to contain a head of a woman, about thirty-five years of age, with beautiful hair. The house- keeper stated that the Abbe had been in the habit of locking himself in his room, and contemplating for hours some object, which it is now suppssed was the woman's head.

div.p: _•,._ CHRISTENING A P RINC ESS.

The infant daughter of the Duke and Duchess of Fife was christened on Thursday afternoon at the German Chat el Royal, St. James's, the officiating clergy being the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Rey. Tynemouth Shore, and the Rev. Canon Sheppard. The infant was named Maud Alexandria Victoria Georgia Bertha, and the sponsors present were the Princess of Wales, the Marchioness of Lorne, the Empress Frederick, the Princess May, the Duke of York, and Sir llorace Farquhar' Bart. Among the others present were the Duke and Duchess of Fife and the Prince of Wales.

".EXCITED POLITICIANS." In The French -Chamber on Thursday M. Mllevoye caused a scene of extraordinary excitement by bring- ing forward his charges against M. Clemenceap of being in league with" British Spies." The House promptly detected the absurdity of the charges, and M. Millevove was constantly interrupted with derisive outcries_ in the result the attack on M. Cleme..ceau broke down utterly ; M. Derotilede, the chief of the" League of Patriots," who had aided M. Millevoye resigned his seat ; M. Milevoye followed his example ; and the Chamber pronounced a severe censure on the latter for the manner in which he had wasted its time by bringing lorward unfounded charges.

A NEW NIINEIIi UNION.

At an important conference of miners held at Aber- dare on Tuesday it was decided to torm a miners' union for South W.Ss and Monmouthshire. Mr. W. Abraham, M.P., (Mahon), was elected president. It was resolved to make a levy of 61. per hexi on all col- lieri-within the district of the union.
SHORT TIME AT THE. CREWE RAILWAY WORKS.

The• London and North-Western Company have decided to put the men at their extensive works at Crewe on short time, work on Niturdays to be wholly stopped. This will affect about 7,030 hands. A number of men also have been discharged. The decline of the traffic receipts is given as the cause of this.

div.head: RAILWAY COMPANIES AND
div.p: THE RAILWAY COMPANIES AND
TRADERS.

For Many years past the various Railway Companies iriGreat Bntain have experienced some considerable difficulty with colliery owners and wagon builders, in relation to the disposition of worn out railway wagons. For the guidance of private wagon Menem they have, after several consultations drawn up a specification, which does not apparently meet the wishes of traders. The intervention of the Board of Trade has therefore been solicited, but the decision of the President is in favour of the Railway Companies. The matter was brought forward by Mr. Powell-Williams, M.P: for South Rirmingham, and Chairman of the Midland Railway Carriage and Wagon Co., Birmingham, in his place in .the House of Commons. He asked the President of the Beard of Trade, whether he was aware that,. whilst Railway Companies were insisting upon compliance,, on the part of private owners of railway wagons with certain costly regulations affecting the construction and repair of such wkgons, they have themselves large num- bers of wagons in regular use which do not conform to those regulations. And, whether he would take steps, by remonstrance with the Railway Companies or others wise, to put an end to such treatment of private owners in ;this respect for the future. Mr. Mundella in reply said he was not aware that Railway Companies were taking the action suggested by the hon. member,.which would appear to be contrary to the terms of section 113 of the Railway Clauses Act, 1845. The Secretary of the Railway Companies' Association had written that the Cempanies do not desire to put the private wagon owners to undue or unnecessary expense, but they are satisfied that when old wagons net up to the require- ments of the specification are so far worn as t..) require substantial replacements, they should be abandoned,and wagons equal to modern requirements be provided. So far as the Companies own stock is concerned,, that practice is undoubtedly followed. The House would understand that in the interests of public safety, all wagons used on railways should be of proper construc- tion and equipment.
This is an important question to owners of wagons, seeing that it affects many thousands of wagon,s now working upon railways.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
THE RAILWAYS DEADLOCK,

At the meeting of the Manchester City Council, on Wednesday, Sir John Harwood made a statement, in which he complained of the delay of the London and North-Western Railway Company in banding over cot- tain portions of their lines which had to be cut througja for the purposes of the Ship Canal, deviation, railways with hig,l3. revel bridges having been constricted by the Canal Company. Mr. Murray said he thought Sir .Dotin had jeopardized the position of the Canal Company by his statement. Sir John Harwood replied that he would not have the secrecy which had characterised the pro- ceedings resting upon him. Let the railways be given up in a fortnight or three weeks, and there- was wattling to prevent the canal being opened next Xanuary. The railways were the one block in the way. THE TRADE BETWEEN LONDON AND SaiL.TPORT.

The managers of the London and Manchester Steam Shipping Company have issued a circular in which they say :.--" We have to announce that after having for about fowr months tried the experiment of sail- ing two steamers per week from London aad Saltport, we find that the result has been to causeqrs a very heavy pecuniary loss, and it is very evident that,, owing to the depression of trade and the slackness usually prevailing during the summer months, the trade, is not yet suffi- ciently developed to justify two sailinga weekly. We I have therefore decided to run only one steamer per week from each end during the summer months, resuming the extra sailings in the autumn."

div.head: WATER FAMINE IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: THE WATER FAMINE IN MANCHESTER.
LIVERPOOL TO THR RESCUE.

At a meeting of the Manchester City Council, on Wed- , nesday,Sir John flazwood,referring to the present water , panic, said if it sliceld be necessary they might ask Liverpool to give them a little water from their system. It was said that Liverpool brought their water from their, Welsh reservoirs, and put it in their Rivington systemc but the engineegat Liverpool said if they gave Manchester water at all it would be from 'Airington. Sir John added that the question had been asked as to why they had at , been able to get water from Thirimere. He would try , to explain. Between Preston and Lancaster the wa.ter- course crossed the Clydesdale Valley. When the pipes were all fired the mountain appeared to be moving, LTA the pipes had so be taken out, at the cost of about £5,000, and put in on a very different principle. A 1 similar state of things had to be dealt with at Troutbeck He was very much ;,watifiecl to know that they might be able to get a little water from Thirlmere for domestic purposes if rain did not come within the nest fifty days, but it would not be wise or safe to rely upon that en- tirely. -

THE CHARGE AGAINST THE WARRING- TON 'BUS COMPANY.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, the two defendants George Gurney, and Thomas Wright were each brought typ on remand on the charge of working a horse while, in an unfit state on the sth inst., and in addition James Kenrick, manager of the 'Bus Company was also charged with allowing the horse to be worked. The details of the case as reported in last week's " Eraminer " were as follows : P.C. Delahay had received a complaint from Inspector Dowty R.S.P.C.A., about the animal, on June 5, and he exam- ined it in ..Buttermarket-street. He found it suffering from a number of raw wounds on the shoulder, chola and crupper. The defendants Gurney and Wright were brought before the magistrates on Monday, the 12th inst., but the.ease was remanded for a week so that the manager could be summoned, as the magistrates were of opinion that he was to some extent responsible for working the horse. The evidence of the previous week was repeated. Kenrick denied that the animal bad any raw wounds at all, and said that if a horse was unfit for work, the driver would tell him and he could then have another horse. He always stopped the men from taking horses which were unfit out of the stables. The Mayor said that the horses which were turned out by the 'Bus Company were a disgrace to the town.—Mr. Kenrick : " That lies with the directors."—lnspector Dowty said that he had been told by the men themselves that they were bound to take the horses out.—Mr. Kenrick : " I maintain they are not."—Mr. F. Monks said that the magistrates were not ignorant of human nature, and they were of opinion that if the drivers exercised their duty in refusing to take out the horses, it would simply mean dismissal. That was the impres- sion on the bench the previous week, and it was a con- dition of things that was intolerable. Mr. Kenrick maintained that the company had the same arrange- ments with their horses as the Corporation had with theirs. The magistrates inflicted a fine ef 2s. 6d. including costs OR Gurney and Wright, and 101. and costs on Kenrick.

div.head: LOCAL VETO BILL,
div.p: LOCAL VETO BILL,
MEETING IN WARRINGTON.

On Monday t-tfternoon .a conference of women temperance workers was held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Schools, Mrs. Roff in the chair. It was decided to form a local branch of the Women's Temperance Federation. In the evening a public meeting was held, at which Councillor H. Roberts, J.P., took the chair. There were also present the Revs. G. A. Bennetts (Connexional temperance secretary), J. lilalan, A. Freeman, and T. Ross, Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., and Mr. I. Hayward. The meeting was opened by singing and prayer. The CHAIRMAN, in addressing the meeting, said that he was no stranger to the Methodists of Warrington. They differed a little theologically, but they were of one mind with regard to the great question of temper- ance. They found that there were people, and very good people too, who questioned the necessity for temperance legislation, and he therefore thought it only reasonable and right co say a word of justification of their policy, as temperance legislators. There were people who said that it was net right to attempt to make a man sober by Act of Parliament, in fact, that a man could not be made sober by Act of Parliament. Anyone who had studied the legislation of this country would see that there were on the Statute Book,Acts of Parliament almost innumer- able, every one of which was dircted to the prevention of men being made drunk in the public-houses of this country.. There were .districts in this country where

incenses for the sale of drink was not allowed, and they chat Jie Men were sober, and therefore they could ha made sober by Act of Parliament. (Hear, hear.) He might mention a district of Liverpool which was en- tirely free from public-houses. There was a population of over 40,000 in this district, and in this district he believed that the poor rate was about half of that of the adjacent districts and the death rate was even less than half. What thAemperance party was contending for was this, that the power which the landlord pos- sessed should also be given to the people. (Applause.) The magistrates who licensed public-houses for populous districts of the towns took very great care that they never licensed any near their residences. The people also ought to have the same protection. There was another point which proved the necessity of legislation upon temperance lines. There was a custom in Warring- ton which was brought from larger towns, of enticing children to certain publie-houses by presenting sweets. This, in some cases, was the means of the children induc- ing their parents to send for drink on some occasions when they would not otherwise do. There ought to be a law preventing any publican from serving anyone under the age of 16 or 18 years at least. Another thing he would mention. Many of them knew of school-fellows and friends, and fellow-business; men, whose hopes bad been miserably shattered by the acquired habit of drunkenness. He might perhaps be a little in advance of some present on that question. When a member of the community had lost his reason, even if he be a harmless lunatic, the law insists upon his removal from amongst his fellows, and provides for his safe custody. If this be desirable for our lunatics, then it was also desirable in the case of men who were going down in every department of life, morally, socially, physically and commercially, and shortening their days. It was necessary for the wives and children of these men that they should be put at least for a time where this habit could not be indulged in. In Warrington, the temperance question was under a great cloud. They were in the centre of the great brewing industry of the district, and this influence was used judicially, and acted largely on the moral senti- ments of the churches. He was thankful that it did not act upon dies enters. He would leave his audience to guess its influence upon the churches, they knew as well as he. He would now come to the question of theatrical licenses. When the County Councils Bill passed, the granting of theatrical licenses was given to the County Councils and the Town Councils. In War- riegton of course it devolved upon the Town Council and from that upon the Watch Committee. Previous to this alteration, they had in Warrington two places which had theatrical licenses, the Public Hall arm the Theatre Royal, Scotland-road. These were granted by the bench with a reservation in each case that there should be no sale of drink upon the premises. This reservation was honourably carried out by the licensees for many years. When the change came and the licensing devolved upon the Watch Committee, the licensees of the Royal Court Theatre, this taking the place of the Public Hall, applied for a full theatrical license, and last year they got the power for the sale of drink. The temperance people were taken by surprise. There was no mcation upon the council notices that the change had taken place. The Royal Court Theatre Company had purchased the Theatre Royal, in Scotland-road. Last March the man who was the licensee of the Theatre Royal applied to the Watch Committee for the renewal of his theatrical license which was granted with the same reservations with which he had held it for many years. When it was sold the purchasers applied last Thursday to the Watch Committee for a full licence,and it was granted wit!) power to sell drink (shame). This was the most disheartening to those who wished to better the town of Warrington. They required the licenses to be reduced, but instead of that being the case, the licenses were increased almost without the slightest trouble. This was too bad and the town Ought to express its opinion about it. The people alone coull alter it. They elected the council and the council elected the Watch Committee, This was not a question of politics, it was a question of morality and Christianity against drink. There were not many in the Council who dared say very much. There were unfortunately too many who were interested directly or indirectly in the drink. The people should watch the men who voted for the granting of these licenses, and take good care that someone cite took their places. (Loud applause.) • The Rev. A. FREEMAN moved the following resolution to be sent to the. House of Commons : " That your petitiouers, recognising to the greater part of the misery and pauperism of this country is indisputably caused by the public-house system, they hear with satisfaction of the introduction in the House of Commons by her Majesty's Government of the Local Control Bill, giving the inhabitants of districts power to veto the issue of licenses by a majority,your petitioners pray your honour- able house to pass the Bill with all possible speed:" He said that a great many men were inclined to criticise the Bill, but he thought that it was their duty to come to the help of those who brought in the Bill, he believed with all sincerity. Mr.R.Ganeerr seconded the motion most heartily. He thought the Bill was a thoroughly English one. The Rev. G. A. BENNETTS in a very powerful speech suppo: ted the motion. He spoke of the large increase in the temperance work during the past two years. During that time the membership of the Wesleyan temperance department had increased 44,000.• Coming to the subject of the Veto Bill, he confessed that at first he was inclined to join the critics, but on examining the Bill he found many excellences. He was ready to accept half a loaf if he could net get a whole one. There were four geed things in the Bill. It recognised the principle of which they had been fighting force many years, namely,popu- lar control over drink. It also gave popular control , over grocer's licenses. He cpncluded with an earnest appeal to those present to do all in their power to help to pass the Bill. 'Hie resolution on being put to the meeting was passed unanimously. A vete of thanks to the Chairman and the Rev. G. lA. Bennet ts was passed, on the motion of the Rev. J. Kirtion, seconded by Mr. Isaac Heyward, to which these gc.ntletnen briefl y replied, and the meeting closed with the pronouncingof tha benediction.

THE ROYAL WEDDING.

Sir,—Don't let Earlestown and Newton be behind other similar towns, in the matter of a loyal and hearty recog- nition of the marriage of our future King to an English born and bred Princess ; and if nothing can be afforded after the strikes and depression in trade for us adults, don't let the children be forgotten. The wedding day and a tea and games or Sreworks would then be an historical landmark tor Chem.—Yours faithfully. YIV.IT REGINA.

div.head: WEATHER.
div.p: THE WEATHER.

-Sir,—The present alarming state of the weather to ' agriculturists and othera,reminds us of past years when the drought caused such disastrous consequences to the nation. We are told by scientists who profess to know (Professor Falb in particular), that we ,need not expect much rain until August or September. If his calculations are correct what are we to do as a nation. I remember how Christians of all sects and pastors have appealed to the Almighty on Sundays for rain, but it bas often been too late, or just when the weather was about to break. I write to remind such people that now is the time to pray for rain, before a national calamity comes upon us. From the reports reaching U 3 from all parts I think it incumbent on the nation to call upon God. We know that if we as a Christian people, in busnility and faith, call upon and make known to Him our needs, He will hear and I verily believe will give us the rain we so much need.—Yours truly, HOPEFUL.

div.head: MONEY.
div.p: MONEY.

Sir,—ln the Runcorn Parish Magazine the " Dawn of Day," Canon Wood complains of the funds for the curates dropping off by nearly forty pounds. He tries to explain, but he never tells them ; " That it is just possible the laity are beginning to get their eyes opened to the trash this Magazine contains.' On page 118 you will find as follows : " For the bread and wine upon the altar do indeed become to the faithful, after the priest has spoken the holy words, the Body and Blood ot Christ. You may go to the altar, and you may receive the Body and Blood of Jesus ; and as you eat and drink, you do really receive Jesus into yourself." Vicars Wood and Blogg might just as well say they become the Sun Moon and Stars when they read the holy words, " I am the light of the world." If so then I may use an old dame's expression, " They want snuffing." Some instructed churchman can. tell us, what baker in Rur.corn and Frodsham these parsons get their bread from, by which this marvellous operation is performed? It is certain Christ had been in bodily existence for over 30 years before the Lord's supper was instituted. How then can these men turn the bread into his body P—Yours truly, VERITY. June 20th, 1893.

A NUISANCE ON WILDERSPOOL CAUSEWAY. Sir,—During a period of 12 years that I have been in Warrington, last Sundy night was the first time that I have come along Wilderspool-road on a Sunday evening. I had been to Hill Cliffe and WAS returning home between sight and nine o'clock. After passing the Brewery there was a large number of persons on the road, maim and female, and on the fence that protects the field sat scores of young fellows whose ages would be from 18 to 20. The conduct of the majority of them was simply dis- graceful while females were passing. I could scarcely, have believed that such a state of things existed as that I saw and heard. I have made it my business to in- quire of persona that have to travel along that road on bunday nights, whether that is the exception or the rule, and I have been informed that it is the rule in the summer months on an evening. My only object in calling attention to this, what I con- alder an abominable nuisance, is to ascertain if it cannot be altogether removed, or that, at any rate, it may be mitigated. I may just add that I did not see a police • Enan on the road till I got to the railway crossing. I don't know whether our Watch Committee have any power in this matter. If so, I for one hope they will use it and so help to remove the cause of complaint. Thank- ing you in anticipation of inserting this in your next Issue.—l remain, yours, Warrington. June 21, 1893.
DECENCY.
THE " LIBERATOR " RELIEF FUND.

Sir,-1 trust yol will give me the opportunity of appealing to those of your readers who have not sub- scribed to the Fund raised on behalf of the sufferers through the "Liberator " frauds. It ia difficult indeed to convey the slightest idea of the great misery that has been brought about by these failures. From every corner of the couutry comes the bitter cry of hundreds of aged people, most of them of our thrifty working classes, bet many having been reared in refinement ; amongst them are a number of invalids. These poor people have lost all their money, upon the interest of which they depended for their daily bread. Some 1,500 of the worst cases have been temporarily relieved and starvation and mental distress staved off for the time being, by a grant from the Fund. When, however, these grans are exhausted, many of the victims will bo as badly off as before, totally incapable of earning a livelihood, and in many cases with other dependent upon them. Those who.are interested in th 2 Fund, however, will not willingly stand by without appealing to the people of England, irrespective of creed or party, to help those aged victims—some of the worthiest of our fellow-subjects—to some sort of per- manent provision fr.r the few years they may have to live. For this, at least £lOO,OOO is required, and would, I think, be at once contributed if sympathetic friends only knew of the p: easing need. £lOO,OOO seems a large sum in itself, but surely if there are not one hundred thousand people who can afford £1 each—there are, at least, 2,000,000 who can spare one shilling each, without missing so small a sum. Some, who could ill afford it, ave nobly assisted the Fund ; in a recent letter, working woman enclosed ss. from herself and her blind sister—although they themselves had lost considerably. Their generous example needs no comment.—l remain, yours faithfully, J. STOCKWELL WATTS. June 20:h, 1893. Hon. Sec.

div.head: SEQUEL TO THE CROFT BREACH OF PROMISE CASE. ANOTHER SCENE IN COURT.
div.p: SEQUEL TO THE CROFT BREACH OF PROMISE CASE. ANOTHER SCENE IN COURT.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday,he- fore his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, an applica- tion for a judgment summons against Wm.Southero, of Croft,was made by Mr.Jenkins,solicito • -m behalf of Mrs. Clough, Croft. The defendant s repre- sented by Mr. A. Browne. The defendant was ordered six weeks ago to pay 14s. per month to- wards the costs—.Eso—of the recent breach of promise action which the plaintiff brought against him. Mr. Jenkins cross-examined defendant as to why he had mot paid,and defendant replied because he was unable.— Mr. Jenkins : Is it true your wife has offered to fay Mrs. Clough £lO if she will let the. matter drop P—l ,don't know.—Mr. Jenkins: Did yoa instruct•your wife to make that offer ?—lio, I didn't.—Mr. Jenkins : Has your wife got any means Except from you ?-.--No.—Mr." Browne : I might mention that the offer of the £lO has been made by the defendant's wile's relatives.—Mr. Jenkins (to the defendant) : N sw• do you say that you are a labourer, with only a few shillings a week that you earn P—Yes,Fve told you that before. —Mr.Jenkins : Do you deny that you have a life interest in an estate.—Yes Ido ; now then.—Mr. Jenkins : Will you swear to that —now be careful, Southern P—l am careful don't you fear—l'm as careful as you.—His rionour : Conduct yourself in a proper way, man—Defendant : All right

In further cross-examinition defendant denied that he held a life interest in the Turret Hall estate which brought him in £3O per annum. He also denied that he collected the rents of eve houses in Heath-lane, and Lord-st. He said the houses were his, but were mortg- aged so much that the mortgagees, Messrs. Snowball, Liverpool, collected the rents of three of the houses to pay the interest of the mortgage, whilst he had to pay the rent of the other two houses, which came to 3s. 85; t )wards other debts which he had contracted. o.le of the debts, was what is called the "bread tax," an ancient tax which was levied at Croft. He said he. had been suffering from chronic rl e :madam for some tune and was going on parish relief next, week.—Mrs. Clough was called. She said that when the defendant was courtmg her—(laughter)—he told h r that be got £22 per year from the Turret Hall estate and drew the rents of five houses. sho believed that he still drew the money from Mr. Buckton, solicitor. The Judge : When did he tell you that.—Just before we got married—(laughter.)—l mean before we ought to have got married (renewed laughter). He stayed, two nights with me on the 2Stb and 29th September, and then he went away on the Ist October and came back 'named to the other lady. (Renewed laughter.) He izn't suffer- ing from chronie rheumatism either.—Defendant : What do you say ?—Plaintiff: You hasn't got the rheumatism. —Defendant : You are a lying hussy !—His Honour: Behave yourself, sir, or I will send you to jail for con- tempt of court.—After a further examination his Hoxour gave an order for the money to be paid in two months, failing which the judgment summons would ha carried into effect.

div.head: fiILETICS.
div.p: A fiILETICS.
NOTES ON GAMES AND
CRICKET.

Warrington first eleven had a disappointment on Saturday in their match with Bolton. In the way of batting everything seemed to go wrong. J. J. Crosfield went out for two ;G. Clarke kept up his unfoitunate season's record and went for 1 ; and three other players failed to score anything beyond what is termed by the Juvenile Man as duck's eggs." The total score was 56, and that included only two individual scone with double figures ; Walton 17, and S. M. Grosfietd 12. R.Smith did not attend—which is generally the case when Warring- ton lose. Bolton managed to plump 114. There was a general disembling of joyful smiles among the Warring- ton spcctators, anyone might know.

Perhaps the match on Wednesday with the Manchester club was about the most interesting of the season. Per- haps it was'nt ; but I think it was. Manchester brought, an excellent team down with them, and were accom- panied by Mr. C.A. N.Hornlsy, ex-captain of Lancashire, and Mr. McLaren, the ex-Lancashire player. Both those' eentlemen took a deep interest in Smith's play—and I wouldn't be a bit surprised if, ono of these days, Mr. Hornby didn't st a what I've seen for a long time, that H. Smith would be useful to the County team. Mr. rHornby by the way, spoke very highly of the Warring- ton ground. B. Smith and 8. M. Crosficld went to the bat first against the howling of Moss, who bowls almost as fast again as Mold ! Crosfield went down for six ; then Su gg came along ; be went out for one ; J. J. Crosfield took up the bat ; but he left with a " ducks egg," and then Clarke the professional came. Pe looked like busi- ness--,and lie slogged away, and scored one. In the meantime Smith had been slashing at it and had now made about 30 runs, when W. Podmore came to the wicket. It was music to the ear to listen to the constant "knocking" that went on now. W.Podmore soon proved himself a conjoint saviour of the game. He made 24 and during Ids innings R. Smith had punished the bowler with the large reputation by making 15 runs in one over, which ccosisted of three 4's and one 3. His total was 24.

At the close of their innings Warrington had picked up a tot al of 155. Manchester came out of the ordeal with 122. Praise should he given to Suzg for the capital bowling performance he gave. Lie has been rather un- lucky this season, so far.

The second team mot the Orford Barracks Sergeant's team on Saturday and scored 150 against 40. Smith, who I believe is brother to R. Smith in the first eleven, came out with a score of 82 for the Warrington second. The full wickets went down fop the Sergeants while for Warring- ten there were only seven wickets.

I said the other week that several of our leading teams woold.have a turn of bad luck. The prophecy has come true. Too true. Warrington were .beaten on Saturday —and en were the Sankey Wesleyans. They met the Widnes White Rosa, but they did not gut beaten much, as one otthe Sankey Wire Mills players said—only by 50 to 19! The bowling of the Wesleyans is said to have been good—but a great many untrue and nasty things have been said about the club, !ately.

The second Wesleyans met the Widnes White Rose second,and beat them by 37 to 26. The victory was largely due to the excellent batting or Elliot and Miles, and also to E.Cotteral's bowling. He took six wickets for ten runs and J. Booth did well in taking four wickets for 12 runs. The Roses brought a gco team, includ'ag a capital bow- ler in T. Baggeridge. After the match the Widnes men did What they always do after a match, sang a number of glees and sacred solos.

After losing their first four matches Sankey Wire Mills • appear to have gbt into their " stride " so to say. Why they didn't get into it before I cannot understand. But they have done it, and that is sufficient. They have not Only wiped off the arrears in runs, but in all matches played lately have had tip-top majorities.

On Wednesday the Wesleyans atoned in some measure ter the severe defeat of the previous Saturday. 11 ley took on the newly formed Penketh Wesleyan team, and beat them by 92 for four wickets, to 57. They had a "sweet thing" on. By the way I do believe on Satur- day there was some dispute going on anent the claim which the Wesleyan juniors have to the title of "Young Lions."

A correspondent writes :—A Cricket League appears to be a popular idea of some of the junior teams. This would be a good thing. A splendid League could be formed of the following junior teams :—Pearson and Knowles, Orford Barracks, Brick-street 3nd Friars-green, Sankey Vresleyaos, S inkey Wire Mills, Grappenhall St. Wilfredo, Lymm, Brewery and others. Judging by the interest caused in football,by combinations of this kind I should say it would be a capital idea to work out.

Walker and Sons Club had their annual fixture with the Burton Brewery Cricket Club, played off on Satur- day. The game ended with 36 runs for each club. The outing was a very enjoyable one to the W..rrington men made especially so by the genial treatment received at the bands of their hosts. They were able to inspect the I brewing establishment of the beer metropolis. They ! bad luncheon and tea at the Station Hotel, in which place a congenial time was spent during the evening. A pleasant feature of the day was the presentation by Mr. Baird, captain of the Warrington team, of a bat, for the highest average score, to Mr. .1. Arber. On the bat was a gold plate bearing the inscription :—Peter Walker and Son, Limited, Warrington Cricket Club. Presented by P. R. Walker, Esq., to .1. Arber. for highest average (12.41 season 1892." The visitors left for Warrington about 11 o'clock. '

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

Abeut 18 members of the Warrington Cycling Club went to Siddington on Saturday. It was very hard riding, and the journey was not particularly enjoyable. A considerable atnount of bathing was done at Sidding- ton before the return journgy was commenzed.

T. A. Edge, of Manchester, the present holder of the 100 and 1,000 miles world's record, started on Monday night from Warrington. with the object of beating J. A. Bennett's 12 hours northern record. No fewer than five of the tyres of the machine he rode punctured. This de- layed him 45 minutes, but he beat the record by six miles. Surely this was a complete success.

div.head: SWIMMING.
div.p: SWIMMING.

At a public meeting, held at the Town Hall on Wedneg- day night, it was decided on the pinosition of.the Rev. H. V. Pigot. to pass a resolution stating the desirability of having a swimming club attached to the new baths. I hope the matter will not be allowed to rest at this re- solution,but that a club will be formedwand that shortly.

div.head: M ISCELLADTF:OtTS.
div.p: M ISCELLADTF:OtTS.

E. Osborne is a promising short distance runner. He captured the first prize in the 220 yards race at the Huddersfield sports on Saturday. and at the same meet- ing, H. Web,ter, Warrington Football Club, came in second in the 300 yards hurdle race, behind C. J. Crocker Bradford, who was given an eight yards start from Webster. In the 120 yards hurdles, the local runner had his chance spoiled by an unlucky fall. At the Stockport R.F.C. and H. Sports, J. Whitfield, Warrington, took the first prize in the mile, with 135 yards start. Whitfield did the distance in 4min. 22 2-sec., and the well-known champion, F. E. Bacon, who was scratch man, would have had to do something above his form to come in a a winner. As it was, he retired in the last lap.

There was a 11. Green of Warrington at the Aspuil P.C. Sports. He turned out in the sprint as" T. Horan, of Warrington," and won it. When found out and warned it is medless to say that he did no more running that day. He is a professional and ran as an amateur.

div.head: Bow Ls.
div.p: Bow Ls.

It was a pleasant trip the members cf the Liberal Club Bowling Club had on Saturday, when they went to Winningtou with the intention of beating that team. Bathe home team demonstrated their &aim to the initial syllable of their name—for they did win. War- rington made 415 against 485. From a list of the storing to be found in another column, it will be seen that the game was practically lost through the turn of bad luck which two excellent players in the Warrington club were visited with. " Another " was especially unfor- tunate for once.

The Bull's Head Club seetn to have what might be termed a sweet thing on with the district League Com- petition. They met and beat the Bone and Jockey Club on Saturday. Tha Bull's Head Club have played four matches and won four and made eight points. The next snore to this is four points for three wins out of four for the Horse and Jockey.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 24, 1893
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 24, 1893
THE PENICETH WATER QUESTION.
A RATEPAYERS' MEETING.

A crowded meeting of the inhabitants of Penketh was held is the Wesleyan schoolroom on Thursday night to consider the advisability of having a better water supply from the village. Among those pre- sent were Messrs. R. Garnett, J.P.,C. B.:Parker,J.S. Snoddy, J. Millington, R. Boardman, T. Wilkinson, R.Cooke,E.CrosP, Hobson, Denton, J.Aitkin,Dignum, J.Routledge, Davenport, etc. On the motion of Mr. Garnett, Mr. Aitken was voted to the chair. Mr. Aitken having explained the purpose of the meeting, invited discussion. . Mr. Parker said he was in a peculiar position as an overseer, and one interested in the water supply. He contended that for a long time the village had been under a serious inconvenience in respect to the supply of water. Some of the wells had been good, but in others there had been a scarcity of water and the in- habitants had had to rely upon the kindness and good- will of their neighbours. In addition to the fact that there had been an inadequate supply of water and that some of the water had been impure, there was the additional fact that the water of Penketh, although it could be got sufficiently for drinking purposes, yet for washing and other purposes it was not good. Although they might laugh a great deal at their friend Mr. Diggle when he mentioned the soap question, there was no doubt that those who had had the luxury of washing themselves with soft water, felt the Penketh water to be very hard. He else contended that where the privies were so near the houses the wells were always in danger of contamination. He would, however, speak specially on the works with which he was connected,the tannery. For the last eleven years they had been short of water for the purpose of manufacture. They had been so in- convenienced in this matter, that for two or three years they had been looking round to see whether 'they could not get a more abundant supply of water, and during the last month or two, they had had to reduce the in- put 'from 1,400 hides a week down to a thousand, and unless the rain continued, they would have to half that.. As a company, they did not wish to reduce their input, and they had made arrangements by which they would have a place .in Liverpool. He was not bringing this forward to create a sensation. He was not merely crying "Wolf." For some time they had men that it wctuld be better In other respects, to be nearer the source of the supply in raw goods, and they had calculated that it would save £5OO a year, in carriage. He would aot have men- tioned these details, but he knew that a great many were dependent more or less upon the works. He thought that they should consider the question in so far as it affected the future welfare of the village. They had come to a crisis in the history of the village, as it was clear that if they could not get a supply of water, the tannery would have to go elsewhere. This question did not only concern the tannery, for other works re- quired water as well, and there was a company a little while age who were contemplating having a works in the township. They had almost made complete ar- rangernenrs, but when the question of the water came I up, they abandoned the idea altogether owin,g to the I lack of supply. Some had suggested to him that they I might get water by boring deeper as had been done in I the Cuerdley township by Sullivan's works, but there was a possibility that a considerable amount of money might be spent in boring, and that they would draw the water of the adjacent wells. The Rural Sanitary Authority had approached the Warrington Corporation asking them on what terms they would be willing to supply the water to Penketh. The Corporation calcu- lated on supplying Winwick water in a twelve inch pipe with which they hoped in time to bring Vyrnwry water to Warrington. The price would be £4OOO, and Penketh was to pay 8 per cent, for that. This however was too expensive and put Warrington entirely out of the ques- tion. The question now was whether Warrington could prevent them from applying to other places for water, and he had it on the authority of Mr. Sutton that it could be obtained independent of Warrington, and that they could apply directly to Liverpool for the Vyrnwry supply. He could not say what terms they could get from Liverpool, but the Ellesmere Local Board had made arrangements for a supply from Ellesmere district and the estimate was £1,300, Ellesmere to pay 7 percent. 23/4 per cent, of which would go towards the sinking fund, and one per cent for the maintenance. As the Vyrnwry pipe was only a mile from Penkoth, he thought they might safely estimate the cost to be similar to Ellesmere. The Tanning Company would take 5,000 gallons a day or even 10,000 a day,as the Vyrnwry water was so good, being almost pure water. Supposing they took 10,000 gallons a day, their bill would probably be over £lOO. No one would be compelled to take the water. Anyone would be free to take or reject it, but it would dspend upon how many took it as to how much the Rural Sanitary Authority. would be deficient in their payment. The maximum charge for water was 2d. per house, and if the amount realised was not sufficient to pay the interest of the money and the charge for the water, the Rural Sanitary Authority would have to charge the deficiency on the township in the rates. Perhaps for some years some portion would have to be collected in rates, but he did not think it would be very great. Mr. Davenport thought that it ought to be proved that Penketh was in any want of water, as there was a large amount of water in the neighbourhood. Penketh was especially favoured in tbis respect They found the river flowing freely (laughter), and there were several brooks, and sometime since the Corporation of War- rington bought some land in Sankey which they believed would be very useful on some future date te eaatilish a watersupply. Considering these points and that even the Tanning Company would be able to get supplied with sufficient water as the Warrington manufacturers got theirs from the river, he thought that it was too expensive to have a fresh water supply brought to Pen- keth. He would not try to put any obstacles in the Iway whatever, but at the same time there were other interests to be looked at.

Mr. R.Garnett to put a definite issue before the meet- ing, moved the following resolution. "That in the opinion of this meeting it is of great importance that some means be taken to obtain a better supplv of water." He was surprised to hear of the place in San- key where the water could be obtained. He had never heard of it before. That however, would make no diff- erence to them. The question was whether it was de- sirable or not to have a better supply of water than they had at present. Some at the meeting seemed to have an abundant supply. Ile had the best well in Penketh, but it was not wholesome as it was so full of lime. Some years ago, Dr. Hurtur was intending to live in Penketh, but when he had a sample of the water he gave up the idea. He might say that he had not washed himself in soft water during the last ten years. Mr. R. Boardman thought that they were going too fast. He did not think it necessary to move in the ques- tion at present. He would like to know how many used gas, and there was a great fuss made about that at the time it was introduced.
Mr. Millington was not going to have any of the water in his property if it were introduced. He main- tained that it would take le. in the E kr rates.

Mr. Turner was of opinion that the water would be for the benefit of the manufacturers and not for the people. Mr. Dignum was surprised to hear from so many quarters that there was plenty of water in Penketh, and that it was so pure and suitable for domestic purposes. For the last six months he had heard personally many complaints about the deficiency of the water and also about its condition. People had complained that their children were under the doctor because of the bad water, and there they were told that there was plenty and that lit was good. The matter was brought before the Sanit- ary Authority because it was considered chiefly as a matter of public health, and they instituted an inquiry into the matter, and the inquiry had resulted in the watcr with one exception being denounced. The Local Government Board would not allow the Sanitary Auth- ority to neglect a matter of public health. Messrs. Hunt, Travis, Seed, Denton. and Roupledge, vigorously opposed the motion, and Messrs. Wilcocks Handles, Ireland, White, Longshaw, wag the Chairman supported it. The moticn was then put to the vote,and 97 voted for and 28 against. The motion was,therefore, declared carried.

Mr. Hobion then moved, and Mr. Parker seconded, that " This meeting pledges itself to do its utmost to secure the Vyrnsvy water as the best water for the pur- pose in the township.”. This was carried with only one dissentient.
After a few remarks by Messrs. Wilkinson and Cross, the business of the meeting terminated.
ALTERATION/ TO THE RECRFIATtON_ GROUND,

Mr.Millington announced that it was intended to have a new gateway to the recreation ground,and also to have seats. This announcement was received with applause. A vote of thanks to the Chairman was passed, on the motion of Mr. R. Cooke.

div.head: MINERS' WAGES.
div.p: MINERS' WAGES.
PROPOSED 20 PER CENT. REDUCTION.

A conference of coal owners was held in .London, yesterday, to consider the question of reducing colliers' wages in all the federation districts. Mr. Chambers presided, and the proceedings were private. The sug- gestion considered was that a fortnight's notice should be given to reduce wages not less than 20 per cent, all round. In the afternoon a deputation from the Miners' Federation met a committee of the Goalowners' Federa- tion. The miners' representatives were Mr. Pickard, M.P., Mr. S. Woods, M.P., Mr. Ashton (secretary), and Mr. Ilowie (treasurer).

div.head: PONTEFRACT ELECTION.
div.p: PONTEFRACT ELECTION.

Mr. T. William Nussey, Liberal, And Mr. Elliott Lees, Cmscreative, were yesterday nominated as candidates for the representation of Pontefraet. The polling takes place on Monday. The Mayor sat at the Town Hall from ten o'clock till noon, and three nomination papers were handed in on behalf of each candidate, no objection being raised. The papers were formally accepted. Both sides held a series of outdoor meetings yesterday.

div.head: WORKINGMEN'S GOSPEL TEMPERANCE
div.p: WORKINGMEN'S GOSPEL TEMPERANCE
MISSION.

Two open-air temperance meetings were hold at the end of Bevvsey-street on Sunday. Mr. J. Drury conducted in the afternoon and Mr. J. Tanner, ig the evening. Addresses were delivered by Messrs. R. Storey, W. Higginson, J. Rigby, J. Tanner, Councillor Dixon, and Mr. H. Taylor (P.C.M.) A number of persons signed the pledge. The usual Band of Hope meeting was held on Monday, Mr. Rose and Mr. Blythe conducting. On Friday night last week, a bible lesson was given by Mr. J. Itigby on " Obedience." In the discussion which followed Messrs. R. Storey, A. Horrocks, Blythe, Drury, Tanner and Clarke took part. On Thursday night a strawberry festival was held, when all present heartily enjoyed the feast provided. A "free and easy" entertain- ment helped to enrich the night's enjoyment. Mr. R. Story presided. Recitations were given by Miss Chas- terworth, Mr. H. Taylor (P.C.M.), and Miss Storey. Speeches were delivered by Messrs. A. Horrocks, J. Drury, J. Tanner, H. Taylor, Trowe, and the Chairman. The hall was beautifully decorated with flowers for the • ;casion.
• ZYMOTIC DISEASES IN WARRINGTON.

SMALLPDX: There has been no fresh centre of infection since the Bth June. There are 11 cases remaining in the Hope Hospital, all of whom are convalescing, so that by the 28th July, the anniver- sary of the introduction ot the disease, it is to hoped the town will be free of the great epidemic of. 1892-93.

'SCARLET FEVER : This disease is also dying out. There are only 20 patients in the Aiken-st. hospital, against 53 last Jnne, and they are all of a mild type. MEASLES : Whilst the two former diseases are disappearing from our midst,this infectious disease has become very prevalent, some hundreds of cases having come to the knowledge of tho Health De- partment. •There have been. 28 deaths from this disease during the past six weeks. tech classes Jones ; 3rd, ST. Pilkington. The Mowing have passed in book-keeping--2nd class, J. Daily ; 3td class, C. Wilkinson. Womersley, M. J. Baxter, J. Houghton, and P. J. Robinson.

div.head: L! MM.
div.p: L! MM.

THE TECHNICAL lI;STITUTE.—The students of the cookery class, held in connection with the Technical Institute, Lynam, recently underwent an examination, the result of which is just issued. Fourteen students entered for the examination, all of whom passed, 13 gaining certificates. The result is very Aatisfactory,and reflects the greatest credit upon the teacher of this use- ful class.

BsrNIVRIZSARY SERVICE:I.-TN anniversary services in connection with the Congregational Church, Lymm, took place on Sunday, the preacher morning and even- ing being the Rev. F. Carter, North wich. There was a large congregation at each service. In the afternoon a cantata was given by the choir. The organist, Mr. J. Leather, Ly rum, officiated with his accustomed ability at all the rervices. The collections taken were in aid of the church.

div.head: PEN BETH.
div.p: PEN BETH.

ORDER OF DRIIIES.—The Ancient Order of Druids' local lodge held their quarterly meeting in the Infants' School, Penketh, on Saturday evening. There was a fair attendance of members. The usual routine of business was gone through, when the officers for the ensu,ng six months were elected. As the lodge was only forry2d six months ago, it has been managed by officers appointed by the Warrington district, and this was the first meeting conducted by officers appointed out of its own members:—N.G.A., Bro. J. Stringer; V.G.A., C. Bartlett; secretary, W. B. Moston ; treasurer, G. Ran- dall; conductor, J. 'Thompson; tyler, I. Heywood ; money steward, G. Willcock • minute clerk, G. Leicester; sick stewards, Bros. W. Woods, J. Swift; bards, Bros. J. Randall, E. Dumbill, H. Horton, E. Molyieux. Bros. T. B. Tetlow, P.A., and P. Dale, P.A. retain their offices as district trustee and delegate. The lodge now numbers 80 members, and is in every respect progressing favour- ably.
