The P.M% J. Yonge preached a special sermon to young men. in Wycliffe Church,.Bewsey-st., on Sunday evening The-subject of the sermon was "Consecration to Christ and Man" as illustrated in the career and work of the late James Gilmour,. missionary in Mongolia. Mr. Yonge took for his text "- He being dead yet speaketh " Hebi Ilc, 4v. In giving a short sketch of the career of Giknour, the missionary, he said James Gilmour was born i in Glasgow in IBS Ife was of humble origin, his father being a mason and a wright. Humble as it was however, it was liohourable, earnest, and religious. James and his brothers were similarly trained to regular and self-denying religious observance. As a schoolboy it was said of him that his natural level was the top of , the class. At Glasgow High Sebool, and afterwards at the University he was always conspicuous for success.. After winning man3r prines at Glasgow University, he entered Edinburgh Theological Hall. In 1887 he entered' Cheshunt College,.having been received as a candidate for missionary work of the London Missionary Society. He sailed to China from Liverpool on February 22, 18V) and arrived in Pekin, on May 18, and soon afterwards began to lay his plans for the Mission of Mongolia,. a territory stretching 3,000 miles from the sea of Japan on theleast to Turkestan on the west, and 900 miles loom the mit ;southern li of Asiatic Russia, to the great wall of , China. The religion of Mongolia is Buddhist, and, the. j larger half of the male population are Buddhist priests. : It was the worrifrous enterprise of converting them to Christianity that Gilmour now attempted. He riseluced himself to their level ; for nearly the whole of he time he lived in Mcrigol tents, and by enduring the hardships, and suffering all the inconveniences of ordinary Mongol life, lie rapidly acquired the .colloquialisms and also made an indelible impression on the natives who ever after spoke of him as "per Gil- mour.". Much of his journeying. in the country was done on foot, and at one time carried about, a tent of his own,. which became not only his dwellinghouse and dispensary but his chapel also. He always endeavoured to instruct everyone who came to him,, confining his preaching to conversations with individuals, and like his Master never scorning a congregation cl one. After a scjcurn in the country for some time he recorded that he had been well received everywhere, but so far as he was aware he had not seen anyone who even wanted to be a Christian. After being among the Mongols alone for shout four years he returned to Pekin where he was married to a Christian lady from England, who after- wards went with him to resume the travels in Mongolia, until the year 1832 when lie had his first furlough to England. On his return, he trade nn e of his most re- markable Mongolian journeys, travelling co foot expos- ing himself to serious risks and dangers. Slung on one s'de of him a postman'a brown bag to told WA kit and

provisions ; slung on the other side an angler's water- proof bag to hold his books ; carrying from a stick over his shoulder a Chinaman's sheep-skin coat, and on his head a stiff broad brimmed hat with lappets inside, tied down over his ears he went forth like a pedlar selling his wares. The long journey terribly blistered his feet : but he hardened himsolf against all such sufferings, and pilgrirnaged on through Mongolia as though it were to lihr. like Canaan was to the ancient patriarch, the veri- table land of promise. It was on this journey that he met with his first convert. In 1885 his wife who had not been able to share his jourseys in Mongolia for some time, sickened with consumption, and on September 19, she died at Pekin, He was left with two sorts, whom he sent home to Scotland for education. An hour after their departure he started on his solitary journey bick to his work. By the close of 1886 he had eqablished three main centres of work which he visited in rotation. His average outlay for food during his residence in his dis- trict was 3d. a day. His last visit to England in 1889 where he remained for eight months. He returned bask to Pekin on March 14, 1890, and was off to Mongolia four days later. He had secured a medical colleague, and entered upon another spell of work in high hopes. He began now to reap a harvest from all his previous work. He baptised many and there was an increased willingness to hear the gospel. Itis work was steadily advancing. The conquest f Mcngolia was actually begun. It was at this time that he was joined by another colleague from Cheshunt College. He returned from Mongolia to Tientsin in April 1891 to preside over the annual meeting of the North China District Commit- tee of the London Missionary Society, and after a brief illness of 10 days he breathed his last. Mr. Yonge con- cluded by urging young men to ponder Gilmour's mes- sage, He spoke to them from his grave in China, and called them to take up the work and carry it on to victory.

div.head: BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: BUILDING SOCIETY.
AT OUR LOCAL CdURCHES, WAIMINGTOA.

WARRINGTON METFIODISM. At the 88th annual meeting of the Independent and Free Gospel Churches, which commenced at Bolton on Monday morning, the Methodist Chapel, Brick-street, Warrington, Was received into full union. WARRINGTON RAGGED SUNDAY SCHOOL. A praiseworthy effort is being made in aid of the above institution, which is not in as flourishing* condi- tion as it deserves to be. On Sunday afternoon the Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) preached a sermon at the Parish Church in aid of the school, and a satisfactory collection was made. Sermons will also be given in aid of the Ragged Sunday School as follows :—June 25, St. Paul's ; July 9, Holy Trinity ; July 18, St. Peters ; July 23, St Barnabas ; July 30, St. Ann's.

RELIGIOUS OPEN-AIR MEETINGS. A series of religieus open-air .-oeetines have been organized by the Free churches of the town, including Wesleyans, Primitive Methodists, Congregationalists, Baptists, Emmanuel Church and the Presbyterians. The meetings are held at River-road and Winwick-road consecutively after the usual evening services in the churches, and are conducted by local ministers. The meeting at Winwick road, on Sunday evening was con- ducted by the Rev. John Yonge who delivered a short address. There were about 300 persons present. HILL CLETE BAPTIST CHAPEL. The Sunday school anniversary and re-opening ser- vices in connection with Hill Cliff Baptist Chapel were held on Sunday. This chapel has almost been re-built, and considerably enlarged. The interior has undergone a complete renovation, and has been re-seated. The total cost of the alterations has been £650. Subscrip- tions have been received amounting to over £4OO, which with the collections raised on Sunday, leaves a balance 'owing of a little over £2OO. The congregations on Sun- day both afternoon and evening were very large. The preacher was the Rev. John Eastern, of Gildersome, Yorkshire. His subject at the afternoon service was " When our children are about us " and in the evening he took for his subject " From North to South." Special hymns and anthems were sung by the choir under the conductorship of Mr. A. R. Kenworthy. The collections which were on behalf of the church, school and renova- tion funds amounted to £53 Bs. THE P.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE. At the P.S.A. meeting in Wycliffe Church on Sunday afternoon there was a larger attendance than usual owing to it being the •quarterly meeting, when ladies were admitted. About 910 persons were present. The Rev. John Yonge presided, and delivered a short address. Mr. A. Parke, J.P., president of the Ashton- under-Lyne P.S.A. was the speaker. He said lie con- sidered the P.S.A. one of the greatest evangelical move- ments of the 19th century. He afterwards referred to the criticisms of the Bishop of Manchester during his recent visit of the Ashton Rural Deanery, in which he described the meetings as " relaxing the Lord's day," as "religious free and easies," as "concerts, entertain- ments and amusements, almost entirely of solo singing interrupted by applause, and that they disturbed the sacred associations of the sanctuary " ; and that they induced children tie desert the Sunday school." The Bishop also advised his clergy to have nothing to do with the P.S.A. movement. Mr. Parke said they would see that the Bishop's address was a carricature and miserable description of the religious character of the P.S.A. meet- ings. With respect to the Bishop's statement that many of the leaders of the P.S.A. movement would fain now , drop them if they could, Mr. Parke said he had thought it advisable to call a meeting of the leaders of the move- Ment in the district at which a protest was unanimously signed, controverting the Bishop's statement. The musical part of the service comisted of an instrumental trio by Mr. J. Roberts, violin, Mr. Pendlebury, clarionet, and Mrs. Pendlebury, harp. Mr. Fieldhouse contributed a solo "Palms." Mr. W. H. Payton accompanied on the organ.
recent

WHAT IS HEAVEN ? The Bev. John Yonge preached on the above subject in Wycliffe Church on Sunday morning. Mr. Yonge said the Christian heaven had been satirized as the place of consummate self indulgence. It was undeniable that the popular idea of heaven was largely that of per- sonal happiness, and might be open to the criticism that it was selfish in its kind. It was thought of as a world of rest, which would be a blessed relief after a life of toil; or as a world of bliss, which would be a most de- lightful exchange for a world of sorrow. The riches of the heavenly life, its glories and its joys were cherished as sweet expectations for those who, poor in this world, found little joy and less glory in their life on earth. And as for its thrones and crowns its palms of victory and harps of melody, its glistening robes, its golden streets, and pearly gates ; all these were far too much thought of in a material sense,and as grounds of exulting hope of personal satisfaction and delight. There was truth in all these ideas, and in many of our experiences in life, it was truth full of comfort. The Master would not have heaven appear any less attractive that oven such ideas could make it. It was a land of rest and riches, and harmony and joy, and in it sin and sorrow had no place. There the wicked ceased from troubling, and there the weary were at rest. They suffered hunger no more, neither thirst any more, neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat. For the Lamb who was in the midst of the throne should feed them and should lead them to living fountains of water, and God should wipe away all tears from their eyes. All this was true, and Christ, the Prince of Heaven would have them in their hours of sorrow freely take the comfort of that hope. But these ideas of heaven, after all were only _elementary and superficial. They were meant far more for comfort.than for satisfaction. • They were certainly net-the only or the principal ideas which we were meant to have in mind. If heaven and its life were dug greater or better than the happy 'reverse of all was unhappy on earth what need would there be for all the manifold precepts and incitements in the New Testament urging us to prepare for its enjoyment? It was clearly preparation far greater than even the forgiveness of sin. None could possibly enter heaven whose sin was unrepented, unforsaken, unforgiven. It might be the case, indeed we might say even that it was the case that some would enter heaven who repent and find forgiveness as near the moment of death as did the thief on the cross and they would thereby find them- selves with Christ in Paradise. Yet surely it did not seem probable or reasonable that heaven to them could , be so heavenly, so homelike, so complete and intense a 1 blessedness as it must become to such as had spent the I earthly life in continual preparation for it. It was no rash or unreasonable speculation to conceive that heaven would be vastly better to the disciple of' years than to the disciple of days. And this for the supreme reason that heaven was a state far mere than it was a place of being, and that its joylconsistod in its characteristic life far more than in any external or visible beauty and glory. We could not conceive of Christ finding a reward for his wondrous life on earth,. with its sorrow and suffering and sacrifice in the mere enjoyment of the sense of glory such as that attached to reigning or even in the mere enjoyment of the accompanying sense of power and dominion. The ;elevation of the. christian who on earth has overcome I himself, to sit with Christ means, the christian elevation to a lofty sphere of heavenly service. It means he is being rewarded by being promoted, and henceforth his reward will be capacity and opportunaty for yet larger ministries of love. Heaven will bring joy to such a christian by introducing hitn to larger liberty, larger power, larger Scope for larger service. In the life to come service will be botb habitual and delightful. The life of heaven is loving service and loving service is heavens crowning joy. SPECIAL SERMON TO YOUNG MEN.

div.head: LATEST NE WS. A BRITISH FLAGSHIP SUNK.
div.p: LATEST NE WS. A BRITISH FLAGSHIP SUNK.
LOSS OF 443 LIVES. ADMIRAL TRYON DROWNED.

The Pres.Ft Association says a startling -rewn-t was received in London yesterday morning to the effect that H.M. battleship Victoria had cone down in the Mediter- ranean, and that 100 lives had been lost. On making inquiries at the Admiralty it was ascertained that the report was correct. The Victoria was the flagship cf the squadron, and was commanded by Admiral Tryon. The Victoria sank alter being in collision with the battleship Camperdown, of the same squadron. The " Central News" says :—The loss of life is about 400, including Admiral Sir George Tryon, commander- in-chief of the Mediterranean fleet ; while a later tele- gram says the Victoria was run down by the Camper- down in raanceuvres. The vessel sank in twelve minutes. Two hundred and forty-five of the crew were saved.

The Press Association has since received the following from the Admiralty :—" Th 9 Lord Commissioners of the Admiralty have received with the deepest regret the following telegram from Tripoli, Syria, from Rear- Admiral Markham Regret to report that whilst manoeuvring this afternoon, ff Tripoli, the Victoria and Camperdown collided. The Victoria sank fifteen minutes after be 80 fathoms of water,bottoin uppermost. The Camperdown ram struck the Victoria before the turret starboard.' "

There were 650 men on board the Victoria, so that about 400 lives were lost. A Portsmouth telegram says that Earl Clanwilliatn received from his son, Lord Gill- ford, the first intimation of the terrible news, Lord Gill- ford being the, first lieutenant on board the Victoria. He has since received a confirmatory message from the Admiralty. The Victoria and Carnrerdown both carried Portsmouth crews, the nvm of the Victoria having been taken out as recently as March last. Most poignant grief is felt at Portsmoulli regarding the fate of Sir Cieorge Tryon and the Portsmouth men, as also that of the crew and officers generally. It is believed that those on deck at the time of the collision alone were saved, while those below perished. Anxious inquiries are be- ing, made at the AdmiraPy by relatives and friends of the officers of the crew.

In February, 1892, the Victoria ran ashore while exer- cising in shallow waters with torpedoes MI the Greek coast. She was, after great exertions on the part of officers and men, got afloat, and being taken to Matto, was found on being docked to have sustained compara- tively slight damage. A court-martial subsequently acquitted her officers of culpable negligence. The Victorii was regarded at the time of the jubilee as the acme of naval architecture, and one of he most interesting of the presents received by her Majesty on that occasion was a silver model of the vessel presented by the navy. The model is now with the other jubilee presents at Windsor Castle, where it excites much admiration.
The Carnperdown is a vessel of 10,600 tons and 11,500 horse-power, and carrying ten guns.
A WARRINGTON OFFICER'S ESCAPE.

In the list of the " Victoria's" officers according to the navy list published at the end of last year; ,the name of Mr. J. S. Place appears. This is Mr. John Spencer Mace, 15 3 ears of age, son of Mr. Elijah Place, Market Inspector, of this town. Mr. Place • joined the " Victoria "on the day in which she stranded on the Greek coast, and he was trans- ferred to the " Collingwood " until the repairs were madegood.when heagainvventonboarilthe"Victoria." He remained on it vmtil he was struck-down bylever, when he was removed to the hospital at Malta and was afterwards invorided home. Thin year lie was transferred to the "tramortalite," on which vessel he is now serving at Bergen. Needless to say, his parents now look wpon his attack of fever as a blessing in disguise. Mr. Charles Dewhurst, another Warrington young officer, is on the Mediterranean squadron, serving: on board the "Victoria's " companion " The Rodney!: A similar coincidence befel Mr. H. E. Grace, who is also mentioned as being a midshipman. on board the" Victoria," he also was invalided home this ' •year and he was transferred•to the " Iti2mortalitd." This gentleman is a son of Dr. W. G.. Grace, the !wall known cricketter;

NTOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next .11 GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on Mown.ty, the 26th day of June Instant, at Half-past Eleven. o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals, arising within the Hun- dreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nant with and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all pri- soners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 26th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the 28th day of June instant, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoun,when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within ths Hundreds of llucklow Mac- clesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last- mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for tho Knu,s- ford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 28th day e,f June instant, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD ports, Clerk of the Peace for the Cour.ty of Chester. Chester, sth June, 1893.

AN OTHER. LARGE TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION. -- A great demonstration in favour of the Direct Veto Bill was held at Greenheys, Manchester, on Saturday. It was estimated that nearly ten thousand people were present. The speaking took place from six platforms, and among others who addressed the gathering were Sir Wilfred Lawson, M.P., Mr. T. P, Whittaker, M.P., Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., Mr, C. E. Schwann, MP., Mr. W. Holland, M.P., Mr. T. Snape, M.P., and Mr. Alderman Ben Tillett. A resolution was passed at each platform hailing with satisfaction the introduction into the House of Commons of the Government Liquor Traffic (Local Control) Bill, and pledging the meeting to render the 'Government every possible assistance in placing the measure on the Statute-book. A petition to Parliament in favour of the bill was also unanimously adopted.

THE EIGHT HOURS BILL. THE PROPOSED SATURDAY SITTING OF THE COMMONS. The canvass of the House of Commons so far for a Saturday sitting to discuss the Eight Hours (Miners) Bill in committee shows that a large number of the Liberal atel Irish members would be willing to give one or two such sittings, but the Conservatives and some of the Liberals who are opposed to the bill will decline to assent to the proposal, and therefore Mr. Gladstone's suggestion cannot be carried out, and the bill will therefore have to stand over to the autumn adjourn- ment, which is now generally acknowledged must take place.
